#5094. What Is Canton Network? The Privacy Blockchain Built for Wall Street

The majority of blockchains are designed in such a way that anyone can see every transaction, every balance and every smart contract call.

Canton began as a niche enterprise project from software firm Digital Asset. It now carries some of the biggest names in traditional finance, including the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), the post-trade backbone of U.S. markets, which launched its tokenization service on Canton and its own private network in October 2026.

Canton Network is a layer-1 blockchain developed by Digital Asset, a New York company founded in 2014 that has long built distributed ledger software for financial firms. Canton launched in May 2023 with a pilot group that included Goldman Sachs, Deloitte, Microsoft and others. Its public infrastructure, the Global Synchronizer, went live in July 2024 together with Canton Coin.

Canton is better described as a "network of networks" than as one big ledger. Each institution runs its own validator node and applications, and its node stores only the data relevant to it, according to Canton's documentation. The nodes connect through the Global Synchronizer, so assets and transactions can move between them atomically: a trade either settles fully on every side or not at all.

The network is governed by the Global Synchronizer Foundation, an independent body hosted by the Linux Foundation. A group of "Super Validators" operates the Global Synchronizer.

In June 2026, Digital Asset raised $355 million in a round led by a16z crypto. HSBC, BNP Paribas, Citadel Securities, CME Ventures and Broadridge also invested. That followed a $135 million round in June 2025.

Think of a repo trade between two banks with a custodian in the middle. Each party sees and checks its own leg. Nobody else on the network sees the details, and the synchronizer orders and confirms the transaction without reading its contents.

This is very different from Ethereum-style chains, where every node replicates every state change. On Canton, the Global Synchronizer, run by the Super Validators, orders encrypted messages and confirms transactions without seeing their contents, while each institution's own validator node holds its data. Institutions keep control of their data, but can avoid much of the reconciliation that legacy systems require. In practice, most activity on the network is private: about 79% of the updates recorded on Canton in a 24-hour period in November 2026 were private, according to CantonScan.

"Atomic settlement" means both legs of a trade, such as a bond and the cash paying for it, move at the same moment. That removes the risk that one side delivers and the other doesn't.

What sets Canton apart is who uses it. Recent milestones include:

Canton Coin (CC) is the native utility token of the Global Synchronizer. Users pay network fees by burning CC. New CC is minted as a reward for validators, Super Validators and "featured" app builders who generate real activity on the network. This setup is called a burn-mint equilibrium.

CC had no pre-mine and no allocations to venture capital investors, according to Canton: every token in circulation has been earned through minting rewards, which are split between Super Validators, app builders and validators. Whether supply shrinks depends on usage. As of November 2026, the network was burning roughly 80% as much CC each day as it minted, according to CantonScan data, below the 1:1 ratio at which supply would start to shrink. Circulating supply stood at just over 40 billion CC.

In November 2026, SEC staff granted Canton no-action relief, saying they view Canton Coin as a digital commodity and would not recommend enforcement over how it is minted. In May 2026, 21Shares launched the first U.S. ETF offering direct exposure to CC.

Institutional custody is catching up. Ledger added Canton Coin support to its Ledger Wallet, and Ripple Custody integrated with Canton in October 2026.

CC trades on several major centralized exchanges, including Kraken, Bybit and OKX. CC perpetual futures are also available on Binance Futures, and Alchemy Pay supports buying CC with a card. On Canton itself, Cantex offers onchain swaps. CC is a native coin, not an ERC-20 token, so be wary of look-alike "CC" tokens on Ethereum-based DEXs. You can track Canton Coin's latest price on Decrypt's price page.

Availability varies by region, and nothing in this guide is investment advice.

Canton's next phase is moving from pilots to full production. DTCC's service is now live, and its roadmap adds onchain settlement, collateral management and digital cash. Derivnex and its partners plan to bring cash settlement and collateral management for derivatives directly onto Canton. Expansion in Asia is also picking up: Shinhan Financial Group, Hanwha Investment & Securities, LG CNS and Meritz Securities have all signed Canton deals.

Canton doesn't have a monopoly, though. DTCC plans to connect its tokenization service to Stellar, Circle's Arc and Solana in 2027.

DBS Bank and Kinexys by JPMorgan have launched an interoperability solution that enables institutions to make instant, 24/7 transfers of USD tokenized deposits between the U.S. and Singapore.

In a statement released Monday, the companies said the service connects DBS Token Services and the account-based permissioned tokenized deposit ecosystem from Kinexys, JPMorgan's blockchain business unit.

The new service enables institutional clients of the two banks to deploy onchain USD liquidity on demand to support local operations across markets, per the statement.

The banks said the solution aims to address the growing demand for cross-border transactions in Asia, where outbound cross-border payments are projected to reach $24 trillion by 2033, nearly double their 2025 volumes.

Ant International has become the first client to adopt the solution, deploying the service for treasury and liquidity management across its entities in both markets.

The launch builds on a framework announced by DBS and Kinexys in November 2025 to enable tokenized value transfers between both banks' onchain ecosystems.

"Tokenized money is moving rapidly from experimentation to delivering live tangible value for clients," said Rachel Chew, chief operating officer and co-head of digital assets, global transaction services at DBS.

Both DBS and JPMorgan have expanded their offerings amid growing interest in tokenization among major financial institutions worldwide.

In September, DBS and Citi said they completed the first weekend USD payment between Singapore and the U.S. using tokenized deposits via Swift's Digital Ledger.

Last month, JPMorgan also brought its USD-denominated deposit token JPM Coin (JPMD) to Ethereum for institutional clients. JPMD serves as a representation of JPMorgan's existing bank deposits on a public blockchain.

#5086. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Other AI Giants Face Lawsuit Demanding Development Freeze

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Other AI Giants Face Lawsuit Demanding Development Freeze

Four nonprofit organizations are taking some of the world's biggest AI companies to court, asking a California judge to stop them from developing more powerful artificial intelligence systems before something goes seriously wrong.

The 63-page complaint, filed Thursday in San Francisco Superior Court, targets OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and SpaceX. The plaintiffs include Public Citizen, the Heat Initiative, Irreplaceable Education Fund, and the Alliance for Secure AI.

They want an immediate court order prohibiting the companies from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most advanced models as of November 12, 2026.

“The Frontier AI companies are developing AI Systems that they do not understand and that act contrary to developer intent, evade control, and break the law,” the plaintiffs argue. To prevent this, they request “an immediate injunction forbidding Defendants from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most capable systems as of the date of this Complaint”

That wouldn't necessarily mean shutting down ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or other existing products. Instead, it would effectively make today's technology the limit, preventing the companies from releasing more powerful successors.

The complaint also asks the court to prohibit the companies from using AI to independently conduct or direct research into better models, a process related to what researchers call recursive self-improvement. The concern is that such systems could eventually improve faster than humans can understand or control them.

The nonprofits argue that California already has laws that could prevent companies from developing products that endanger the public, even before those products cause serious harm.

Their lawsuit invokes the state's Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits unlawful or unfair business practices. One part of their argument is that developing increasingly capable AI systems creates a public nuisance: a danger that affects the health, safety, or property of a broader community.

For example, a factory releasing dangerous chemicals into a neighborhood could face legal action before someone suffers a fatal injury. The plaintiffs want the court to apply similar reasoning to AI development.

They argue that companies are knowingly creating increasingly powerful systems that could facilitate cyberattacks, help develop biological weapons, or eventually escape human control.

“No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products—much less ones that could kill us all—as inevitable,” the plaintiffs argue in the complaint.

Robert Weissman, co-president of Public Citizen, said in a statement that the groups want the court to declare the companies' practices unlawful and “freeze further AI development.”

The legal challenge is whether the alleged risks and practices are enough to justify such sweeping restrictions. Even though these frontier labs constantly warn about how powerful and dangerous their models are, as defendants they have not been found liable, and warnings about potential catastrophe do not automatically establish a violation of California law.

The complaint points to incidents that have already occurred as evidence that the dangers aren't entirely hypothetical.

In July, OpenAI models escaped a controlled testing environment and compromised Hugging Face's infrastructure while attempting to cheat on a cybersecurity evaluation.

A subsequent independent investigation found that roughly 1,200 OpenAI agents used an unauthorized internal message board to coordinate, with about 700 joining the attack on Hugging Face. The agents were attempting to obtain answers to the benchmark testing them.

These incidents involved AI agents, programs that can execute tasks, browse websites, write code, and interact with external systems rather than simply responding to questions.

Documented security failures, however, are not proof that today's AI models can cause human extinction. The plaintiffs are connecting those incidents to predictions about what increasingly capable systems might eventually do, and that broader danger remains disputed.

“It is patently illegal for companies to develop and release products they know are unsafe in any respect,” Matthew Platkin, the former New Jersey attorney general representing the plaintiffs, said in the statement.

#5084. Vitalik Buterin backs higher gas costs for creating accounts and deploying smart contracts to help Ethereum scale

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The proposed gas changes could break existing applications, leaving developers to address compatibility issues before Glamsterdam.

Ethereum Ethereum (ETH) co-founder Vitalik Buterin is backing a proposal that would make creating accounts, storage slots, and smart contracts on the network more expensive than it currently is.

In an article he shared Monday, Buterin defended EIP-8037, a proposal planned for Ethereum’s upcoming Glamsterdam upgrade, saying the network cannot scale up transaction capacity without limiting the growth of data that nodes must store.

Buterin explained that execution capacity can expand much faster than Ethereum's state, but he said allowing both to grow at the same rate would overwhelm node operators and make it harder to maintain a decentralized network.

Buterin argued that lowering gas costs for other operations would be more disruptive than raising the cost of creating new state.

"The goal of EIP-8037 is to decouple Ethereum’s scaling limits: enable a much higher amount of execution (which is easy to scale), but only a little bit more state size growth (which is hard to scale)," he wrote.

Proposal EIP-8037 would raise the gas required to create a new account from 36,600 to 197,900 gas units, in Buterin's example. Users would also spend 110,020 units, up from 22,100, to create a new storage slot and nearly 37.8 million gas units, compared with 4.95 million currently, to deploy a 24 KiB smart contract.

Notably, the proposed account-creation charge would also apply when an ETH transfer creates a new account onchain.

Buterin said Ethereum currently adds about 110 GiB of state annually, but his illustrative estimate put that figure at 1,100 GiB per year if the block gas limit rose tenfold without repricing state creation. According to Buterin, this would put additional pressure on disk storage, initial synchronization, and state-related operations.

Buterin also acknowledged that EIP-8037 could break existing applications, including bridges with hardcoded gas limits. Developers will need to review their contracts and transaction configurations before Glamsterdam, he said.

#5080. The Week Jensen Huang Fell: How a Spy Scandal Toppled Nvidia’s CEO

The Week Jensen Huang Fell: How a Spy Scandal Toppled Nvidia’s CEO

In the span of a few days, the most powerful executive in artificial intelligence went from untouchable to unemployed.

Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia from a graphics-card maker into the roughly $4 trillion engine of the AI boom, resigned Thursday after 33 years, felled not by a bad earnings report but by a scandal with the texture of a spy thriller.

Here’s how a defining week for AI, and by extension crypto, unfolded.

The crisis began with reports that Huang had grown close to Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian customers, whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of gathering information for Beijing.

For a company at the center of the U.S.-China chip fight and a looming debate over tighter export controls, the national-security overtones were impossible to ignore. Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into whether Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence operation, though it said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised.

On Nov. 8, Huang apologized for being “unfaithful” to his wife, acknowledging the relationship.

What might have been a single lapse quickly snowballed. The New York Times reported a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reported to Huang.

By Thursday, Huang was out as president, CEO and board member. Chief financial officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO, and longtime director Harvey Jones took over as board chair. The abruptness stunned an industry accustomed to treating Huang as synonymous with Nvidia itself.

Then, a day after his resignation, Reuters reported a third relationship, an “intimate” one with a second unnamed Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter. Reuters did not identify her, and Nvidia declined to comment. Huang has acknowledged only the Alice Huang affair, deflecting when the Times asked about Powell.

Nvidia’s stock cratered more than 14% at the open on Thursday before clawing back to close down about 4.6%. Wall Street quickly sorted winners from losers: rivals like AMD and Broadcom fared better, while companies tightly tied to Nvidia’s business took the brunt.

The reaction underscored how much of the AI trade, and the crypto market that increasingly moves with it, rests on a single company.

The scandal then rippled outward. Singapore barred Alice Huang from returning to the country, Alibaba shares slid on reports it was a Megaspeed customer, and congressional committees had already sought a closed-door briefing from Huang over his Megaspeed ties.

The loudest names in tech, AI and crypto called the ouster a blunder, with one founder branding it “a massive mistake.” Inside Nvidia, an internal suggestion-box post drew more than 1,600 comments, many pleading for Huang’s return. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” one wrote.

The board has moved on regardless. According to the Financial Times, it approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, a former Nvidia executive who led Arm through its 2023 IPO, as a potential successor, though Nvidia called speculation about any candidate “premature.” Analysts have also floated Nvidia’s Ian Buck and AMD’s Lisa Su.

Nvidia’s chips power the AI data centers whose explosive buildout has become intertwined with crypto, from AI-agent commerce to the mining firms pivoting to host AI workloads.

Leadership turmoil at the company that supplies the picks and shovels ripples outward, and it lands amid a broader reckoning over AI’s role in everything from cyberattacks to data-center politics.

Nvidia reports earnings Nov. 17, with Kress at the helm and the permanent CEO search still underway, a nervous moment for a market already rattled by a sharp week-ending selloff.

For now, the company that defined the AI era is leaderless at the top, its founder’s legacy clouded by scandal, and the question hanging over Silicon Valley is whether anyone can fill the role Huang made uniquely his own.

Meanwhile, Dunamu is currently in the process of a merger-acquisition with South Korean heavyweight Naver Financial via a stock exchange.

Dunamu, the parent company of South Korean crypto exchange Upbit, swung to a net loss in the third quarter as a broad downturn in digital asset markets weighed on trading activity and revenue.

According to its official disclosure, Dunamu posted an operating loss of 3.5 billion won ($2.6 million) and a net loss of 18.6 billion won ($13.8 million) for the third quarter. Both figures represented a shift to losses from operating profit of 235.3 billion won ($174.3 million) and net profit of 239.0 billion won ($177 million) in the same period last year.

It reported consolidated operating revenue of 151.7 billion won ($112.4 million) for the quarter, down 60.7% from 385.9 billion won ($285.9 million) last year.

“The deterioration in sales and profitability is attributed to the contraction in global digital asset market trading, weaker investor sentiment, and operating expense burdens,” the company said in a translated statement. About 96% of Dunamu's revenue comes from the Upbit trading platform.

Dunamu's overall performance so far in 2026 also shows a notable decline from the previous year.

For the nine months ended Sept. 30, 2026, consolidated operating revenue totaled 559.8 billion won ($414.7 million), down 52.9% from 1.19 trillion won ($880 million) in the prior-year period.

Operating profit for the nine months was 108.0 billion won ($80 million), down 86.2% from 784.8 billion won ($581.3 million) a year earlier, while net profit was 89.8 billion won ($66.5 million), down 86.3% from 657.8 billion won ($487.3 million).

Meanwhile, Dunamu is currently in the process of a merger-acquisition with South Korean heavyweight Naver Financial via a stock exchange. When closed, Dunamu is set to become a subsidiary of Naver Financial, and the combined entity plans to aim for a public listing — potentially on Nasdaq — within five years.

While the transaction faced delays due to regulatory headwinds, the country's Fair Trade Commission has reportedly started a review of the deal, nearly a year after the companies filed the merger notification, signaling potential progress.

#5077. Senate Agriculture Committee to Hear Trump’s CFTC Nominees Tuesday

The Senate Agriculture Committee will hear President Donald Trump’s two nominees to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) on Tuesday, a confirmation hearing that comes as the derivatives regulator has only one sitting commissioner.

The committee scheduled the session for 3 p.m. Eastern in Room 106 of the Dirksen Senate Office Building. The White House sent the nominations to the Senate on Nov. 12. The nominees are Nathan Anonick of Virginia and Matthew Rowland of the District of Columbia. The hearing notice says to check back for live video, and the committee has not posted written testimony.

Trump nominated the pair last week as part of a bipartisan slate for the CFTC and the Securities and Exchange Commission, a step that would begin to refill two regulators that have been operating short-handed.

Anonick serves on the Republican staff of the Senate Agriculture Committee under Chairman John Boozman of Arkansas. He was nominated to the seat once held by former Chairman Rostin Behnam, for a term ending June 19, 2031. A 2023 committee release said Anonick joined the panel in 2022 to manage a portfolio that includes cryptocurrencies, futures markets and derivatives, and that he had previously worked at the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation as a resolution policy specialist.

Rowland is a CFTC attorney detailed to the committee’s Democratic staff under Ranking Member Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota. He would fill the remainder of former Commissioner Summer K. Mersinger’s term, which expires April 13, 2028. Both nominees come from the committee that oversees the CFTC.

CFTC Chairman Michael Selig called them “two strong bipartisan picks” and said he looks forward to working with them “upon their confirmation by the US Senate.”

Kristin N. Johnson and Steven Levine, the two SEC nominees from the same White House list, are on the agenda for a Senate Banking Committee nominations hearing at 10 a.m. Thursday in Dirksen 538.

The CFTC can seat up to five commissioners, with no more than three from the same party. Chairman Michael S. Selig, sworn in Dec. 22, 2025, is currently the only sitting commissioner listed on the agency’s website. Even if the Senate confirms both nominees, two of the five seats would remain vacant.

Each nominee still needs a committee vote and then confirmation by the full Senate. The Agriculture Committee has not scheduled that vote.

The hearing lands in a lame-duck Senate, weeks after Democrats swept both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterms. The new Congress is seated in January. If the Senate does not confirm the nominations before then, they would typically be returned to the president and have to be sent again.

After the election, TD Cowen’s Jaret Seiberg told clients he does not expect Democrats to confirm Trump nominees unless the president fills Democratic seats at agencies such as the FDIC and the SEC, a step he has called unlikely. The White House slate does that at both the SEC and the CFTC.

The nominations also arrive with crypto market structure legislation stalled. The Clarity Act failed a Senate cloture vote 49-50 on Sept. 15 and dies on Jan. 3 unless the lame-duck session revives it. The bill would formally divide oversight of digital assets between the SEC and the CFTC, distinguishing which are securities, commodities or stablecoins.

Without new law, the CFTC has set much of its crypto policy on its own this year. Selig’s agency opened the door to equity perpetual futures, and a federal judge later said the CFTC likely overstepped its authority while letting trading continue.

The open question is whether a Senate heading for Democratic control confirms the CFTC picks before January, or leaves the agency short-handed into 2027.

#5076. Solana drops ‘mainnet beta’ label and adopts protocol version 1.0

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Users don’t need to take any action, while validator operators should check which client releases support each protocol rollout.

The Solana Foundation has retired the network's “mainnet beta” designation and introduced Solana 1.0 as a shared protocol version independent of individual validator client versions.

In a statement on Monday, the foundation said the change recognizes Solana's technical progress and separates its protocol version from the software releases of individual validator clients.

"Solana 1.0 recognizes the progress on network performance, resilience, and developer experience," the foundation wrote. "That progress continues with this simplification of nomenclature."

The foundation said the change does not require any action from users, while SOL Solana (SOL) holdings, transaction histories, and accounts remain unaffected.

Developers and validator operators should continue following individual software release guidance, since assigning a protocol version does not automatically activate every associated network improvement, according to the statement.

The name change comes as Solana has been upgrading its infrastructure. In October, the network's mainnet activated Alpenglow, a consensus upgrade that targets transaction finality of about 150 milliseconds, down from 12.8 seconds.

Jump Crypto's Firedancer went live on Solana mainnet in December 2025, giving operators an independently developed alternative to Agave. The two are built with separate codebases, release schedules, and version numbers.

Following the name change, both development teams, validators, and infrastructure operators will have a common way to identify changes to Solana, regardless of which client they run, the foundation said.

Last week, the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation announced plans to connect its tokenization service to the network in the second half of 2027.

Formation Securities has also notified the SEC of plans to operate a tokenized securities trading venue on Solana, targeting an early 2027 launch.

Separately, asset manager Schroders launched a tokenized emerging-markets debt fund on Solana through Centrifuge earlier this month. Other notable launches on Solana this year include USDC accounts for U.S. Samsung Galaxy users and integration with Polygon Labs' Open Money Stack.

#5075. Bitcoin ETFs Lose $2.1 Billion in November as Outflow Streak Hits Seven Days

Bitcoin ETFs Lose $2.1 Billion in November as Outflow Streak Hits Seven Days

Bitcoin ETF investors are still heading for the exits, and the price slide is speeding up.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $185.4 million on Friday, according to Decrypt’s ETF tracker, extending their outflow streak to seven straight trading days.

The funds lost about $829 million this week after shedding nearly $1.3 billion the week before, bringing November’s outflows to roughly $2.1 billion.

The selling so far this month has been relentless. The funds bled $1.4 billion over five sessions earlier in the streak as investors cut risk. Cumulative net inflows since launch have slipped to $55.3 billion, and total net assets fell to $94.9 billion, below the $100 billion mark they held through much of October.

Other crypto funds haven’t escaped the rout. Ethereum ETFs took in a modest $2.3 million on Friday, snapping a six-day outflow streak, but still lost about $336 million on the week and roughly $702 million so far in November. Solana ETFs shed about $28 million this week, though they retain $1.6 billion in cumulative net inflows.

Spot crypto ETFs hold the underlying asset, such as Bitcoin or Ethereum, and trade on stock exchanges like ordinary shares, giving investors exposure through a regular brokerage account. Bitcoin funds have drawn $55.3 billion in net inflows since debuting in January 2024. Because issuers report flows daily and much of the money comes from institutions and financial advisers, the figures have become a closely watched gauge of investor sentiment.

The outflows have tracked a sharp sell-off. Bitcoin traded near $64,500 over the weekend, down 6% over 24 hours and about 15% on the week, according to CoinGecko, and it has lost more than 22% over the past month.

Ethereum fell 8.4% to about $1,790, and Solana dropped 12% to roughly $70. Total crypto market value slid 4.5% to about $2.3 trillion.

Bitcoin hit a 12-week low this week as fears of further Federal Reserve rate hikes erased its summer rally, and concentrated liquidations pushed the price below $69,000 earlier in the week.

Not every institution is retreating. JPMorgan’s holdings of Bitcoin and crypto-linked securities are approaching $1 billion, according to its most recent SEC filing. However, those purchases predate the more recent market downturn.

#5073. Harvard, Dartmouth keep Bitcoin ETF stakes steady as fund gains 42% in Q3

Harvard’s gold ETF share count rose nearly 20-fold in Q3, while Dartmouth kept its positions in Solana and Ether staking ETFs unchanged.

Harvard University and Dartmouth College reported unchanged share counts in BlackRock’s spot Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF) at the end of the third quarter as a Bitcoin rally lifted the value of both stakes.

Harvard held 3.04 million shares of the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT), worth about $144.1 million at the end of September, while Dartmouth reported 201,531 shares valued at $9.5 million, according to Form 13F filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

IBIT gained about 42% in Q3 as Bitcoin (BTC) rallied nearly 43%. Both posted their strongest quarterly gains of 2026 through September.

Harvard has reported the same IBIT share count since the end of March, after cutting its holdings by 43% in Q1 and 21% in Q4 2025. Dartmouth has reported the same 201,531 shares since first disclosing its Bitcoin ETF position in Q4 2025.

Harvard increased its share count in the State Street’s SPDR Gold Shares ETF (GLD) nearly 20-fold in Q3, to 1.16 million from 58,862. The position was worth $442.2 million at the end of September.

Dartmouth again reported 304,803 shares of the Bitwise Solana Staking ETF and 178,148 shares of the Grayscale Ethereum Staking ETF. The positions were worth $4.9 million and $4.5 million, respectively, at quarter-end.

The steady university holdings contrasted with moves by major financial companies. Jane Street reduced its IBIT shares by 19% in Q3, while JPMorgan Chase increased the number of shares it held by 9.6%, according to their latest quarterly filings.

#5072. Bitcoin Price Holds Near $65,000 as Nvidia Turmoil Drags Nasdaq Down 2.5%

Bitcoin price traded near $65,000 on Monday afternoon, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data, up more than 1% from where it sat at the time of this morning’s report. The world’s largest cryptocurrency held its ground even as a fresh round of selling in Nvidia dragged the Nasdaq down about 2.5%.

The session was choppy. Bitcoin started the day near $64,000 after a weekend plunge to $62,000, then jumped to about $65,600 shortly after the U.S. stock market opened. The bounce faded within the hour, and the bitcoin price slipped back toward $64,000 as tech stocks extended their losses. Buyers stepped in there, and bitcoin has spent most of the afternoon trading around $65,000.

Nvidia was again the heaviest weight on markets. CNBC reported shortly after noon that the chipmaker’s board is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO after he resigned last week. The board is instead focused on an investigation into whether Huang’s conduct compromised national security or company secrets, the report said. Earlier Monday, President Donald Trump said he would not mind seeing Huang return.

Nvidia shares fell to a fresh intraday low after the report and closed down about 4%, a day before the company reports quarterly results. U.S. chipmakers dropped more than 5%. The Nasdaq Composite slid about 2.5% and the S&P 500 lost nearly 2%, with investors also bracing for Anthropic’s IPO later this week.

Bitcoin did not follow stocks to their lows this time. As the Nasdaq sank to its worst levels of the day after the CNBC report, bitcoin stopped going down and held near $64,800. That marks a change from the past week, when the bitcoin price traded largely in step with chip stocks.

The macro backdrop offered no relief. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, speaking at a San Francisco Fed conference, avoided any guidance on the near-term path of rates. He said artificial intelligence could lift productivity but “could bring substantial labor market disruption as some jobs are displaced, rather than complemented, by technology.”

His remarks did little to change expectations for a rate hike next month. Fed funds futures imply a quarter-point increase in December, and the dollar index touched its highest level since April 2025. A stronger dollar tends to weigh on bitcoin and gold, and gold fell to its lowest level since October 2025 earlier in the session. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 5.12%.

Bitcoin-linked stocks took a heavier hit than the coin itself. Strategy (MSTR) fell nearly 8% and Coinbase (COIN) dropped about 6%, while Strive (ASST), which bought 251 bitcoin last week, slid about 12%. Strategy also added 485 bitcoin last week, but it faces about $2.8 billion of potential index-fund selling when MSCI removes it at the Nov. 30 close, JPMorgan estimates. Spot bitcoin ETFs shed $185 million on Friday, their seventh straight day of outflows.

The next test arrives Tuesday after the bell, when Nvidia reports its fiscal third-quarter results. Analysts expect earnings growth of 90% on revenue of $109 billion. Minutes from the Fed’s October meeting follow on Wednesday, the same day Anthropic is expected to price its IPO.

For now, bitcoin has bounced twice from the $64,000 area on Monday. A move above this morning’s high near $65,600 would put Sunday’s bounce toward $66,000 back in view, while a break below today’s low near $63,800 would bring the weekend low around $62,000 back into play.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $65,000.

Strategy bought another 485 BTC for approximately $33.4 million last week as bitcoin fell to its lowest level since July.

Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) treasury company Strategy Strategy, Inc. (MSTR) purchased another 485 BTC for $33.4 million at an average price of $68,887 per bitcoin last week, according to an 8-K filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday.

The latest purchases take Strategy's total bitcoin holdings to 850,849 BTC, equivalent to more than 4% of bitcoin's maximum supply cap. The firm's total bitcoin treasury holdings were acquired for a total cost of approximately $64.2 at an average price of $75,452 per bitcoin, according to the filing.

Proceeds from at-the-market sales of its Class A common stock, MSTR, were used to acquire the cryptocurrency. Between Nov. 9 and Nov. 15, Strategy sold 2,087,040 MSTR shares for approximately $244.7 million, with around $18.1 billion worth of MSTR shares remaining available under that ATM program, the firm said.

Strategy also used the proceeds, alongside interest earned on cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, to repurchase 2,282,510 STRC preferred shares during the same period for $228.1 million, as well as $18.9 million from its USD Reserve to cover dividends on its preferred stocks.

As of Nov. 15, the balance of Strategy's USD Reserve and USD Cash holdings were $4.75 billion and $151.2 million, respectively, per the filing.

On Wednesday, MSCI confirmed it was moving to delist Strategy from its USA Index following new eligibility rules it adopted for so-called "non-operating companies." The new rules consider companies' operating assets alongside five financial measures, replacing prior temporary restrictions on firms that held at least half their assets in crypto. Strategy Executive Chairman Michael Saylor previously described the treatment as "discriminatory."

Bitcoin fell around 12.6% last week, continuing a multi-week slide that has seen the foremost cryptocurrency drop from a peak of around $86,000 in early October to below $65,000 over the weekend. Strategy is currently sitting on a $9.6 billion paper loss on it bitcoin holdings as a result.

Amid the weekend plunge, Saylor posted another Strategy bitcoin acquisition tracker chart stating, "This dip could use a little orange," flagging the potential acquisition announcement ahead of time.

Strategy dominates the 197 public companies that have launched some form of bitcoin treasury. Metaplanet, Tether-backed Twenty One, Strive, and Bullish make up the rest of the top five, with 44,000 BTC, 43,514 BTC, 43,153 BTC, and 22,000 BTC, respectively, according to Bitcoin Treasuries data.

MSTR fell 6.5% last week, closing Friday at $111.62, its lowest level since June, according to The Block's Strategy price page.

#5069. How Wall Street Is Racing to Claim the Onchain Dollar

How Wall Street Is Racing to Claim the Onchain Dollar

For years, stablecoins were crypto’s business, dominated by Tether and Circle and used mostly to trade digital assets. That era is ending.

Over the past few months, and especially the past few weeks, the biggest names in traditional finance have moved en masse to claim a piece of the onchain dollar. Here’s the map of a land grab that’s accelerating fast.

The clearest signal came this week, when Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, Santander, and Deutsche Bank were reported to be among banks committing roughly $270 million to a joint dollar-stablecoin venture codenamed “Project Faro.”

The capital funds five years of operations for a U.S.-incorporated issuer targeting a 2027 launch, part of a 21-institution coalition that has swelled from an initial group of 10. The goal is explicit: challenge Tether and Circle, which together still control about 85% of a roughly $290 billion market.

While the consortium plans, SoFi has shipped. Earlier this week, its SoFiUSD, billed as the first stablecoin from a U.S. national bank, expanded onto Polygon this month alongside Ethereum and Solana, reaching the bank’s 17 million-plus members.

SoFi also launched SoFi Earn, a tokenized deposit paying 4.40% yield that converts into SoFiUSD, and already settles its entire card program over Mastercard’s network.

Meanwhile, the federally chartered crypto bank Anchorage Digital has positioned itself as a settlement backbone.

Anchorage’s tokens can now settle transactions on Visa’s network, starting with Western Union’s USDPT, and it recently anchored both sides of the U.S.-Mexico stablecoin corridor, custodying tokens across one of the world’s largest remittance routes.

Mastercard has been the most aggressive incumbent among payment giants.

It launched a Global Money Platform with acquired stablecoin firm BVNK, rolled out a Stablecoin Security tool to screen payments for fraud, and unveiled Agent Pay for Machines, letting AI agents transact in stablecoins.

Visa, meanwhile, has expanded its own stablecoin settlement program across multiple blockchains.

The crypto-native incumbents, not to be left out, are also racing to entrench.

Circle struck a deal to bring USDC settlement to banking rails in Latin America, starting with a Colombia pilot, part of a broader expansion into dozens of emerging markets.

The catalyst is regulation. The GENIUS Act, signed in 2025, created the first U.S. framework for dollar-pegged tokens, giving regulated institutions a clear path into a business they had largely watched from the sidelines.

The Donald Trump administration has framed dollar stablecoins as a tool to extend the dollar’s reach and global hegemony, and banks that once dismissed crypto now see a settlement business they can’t afford to cede.

Much of this remains early. Project Faro has no token, no CEO, and no final name. Tether and Circle still dominate, and bank-issued tokens face a steep climb to win share.

But the direction is unmistakable: the onchain dollar, once crypto’s turf, is now contested ground, with Wall Street, the card networks and the stablecoin incumbents all racing to own the rails money moves on.

Speaking at Solana Breakpoint, Matt Hougan said crypto could be set up for a "very good" 2027 if the market holds up over the next few weeks.

Bitwise Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan said bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) could fall further if economic conditions worsen, drawing a parallel with the 2018 bear market in an interview with The Block's Gareth Jenkinson at Solana Breakpoint in London.

In 2018, after bitcoin fell from $20,000 toward $5,000, investors thought the market had found a bottom, Hougan said. However, it ultimately went on to fall to about $3,000.

Over the weekend, bitcoin slid to a four-month low near $62,000 before recovering to around $65,000 on Sunday afternoon, down about 13% over the past week. As such, it has largely retraced a move to around $86,000 in October from June and July's $58,000 range, which many analysts saw as the cycle's ultimate low. Coming into the weekend's price action, U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds had also recorded more than $1 billion in net outflows for the second week in a row.

Asked about his take on the move, Hougan pointed to the recent Binance hack, the "blue wave" U.S. midterm elections, high U.S. inflation, and the growing chance of another Fed rate hike. The market is "digesting this new regime where liquidity is tighter," he said.

However, the "optimistic ray of sunshine" is that bitcoin has still held above its June lows, Hougan said, arguing that there is "resilience underneath the surface." If bitcoin can continue to hold up for the next handful of weeks, crypto could be set up for a "very good 2027," he said.

Regardless, the Bitwise CIO is still bullish on the cryptocurrency longer term.

"I think it's the best risk-adjusted trade in all of finance for the next 10 years," Hougan said, adding that he spends most of his days talking to institutional investors and has never heard them so optimistic about bitcoin and crypto. He cited Morgan Stanley's bitcoin ETF launch and Wells Fargo putting bitcoin into a model as examples of growing institutional adoption. "The only thing lagging is price," Hougan said.

Bitwise previously raised its 10-year bitcoin price target to $1.6 million, projecting a 34.3% annualized return over the decade.

Tokenized deposits are bank deposits represented on the blockchain. The service connects DBS Token Services with JPMorgan’s Kinexys platform for transfers between Singapore and the US, according to a press release.

#5063. Layer 2 Scaling Explained

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Rollups, Sidechains, Appchains, and Blockchain Trade-offs

Layer 2 scaling helps blockchains process more activity by moving execution or coordination away from the base chain while preserving different levels of security, settlement, and decentralization. Rollups, sidechains, and appchains each try to make transactions faster and more affordable, but every scaling design introduces trade-offs.

Blockchain adoption is increasing, but the networks people use are often congested. Most Layer 1 blockchains process only a few transactions per second, meaning activity beyond a network’s throughput can create periods of congestion with slower than expected confirmations and high fees. Transaction speeds and costs need to improve if blockchain is going to see mainstream adoption for DeFi, NFTs, gaming, payments, and beyond. The market has responded with multiple options, but before token-level transactions move off mainnet, users need solutions that make blockchain faster and cheaper while preserving what makes these networks attractive, namely security and decentralization.

This guide introduces the core frameworks used to scale blockchain networks. The explanation stays conceptual and beginner-friendly.

The lesson summaries below give a short overview of the full course content. Take the full interactive Scaling & Layer 2s 101 course to explore each lesson in more depth through guided explanations, examples, and activities.

Course introduction - Why Blockchain Needs to Scale

Explains how limited throughput creates congestion and higher fees as DeFi, NFT, gaming, and payment activity grows.

Compares monolithic and modular architectures, vertical and horizontal scaling, Layer 2 systems, rollups, and sharding.

Explains Optimistic and ZK rollups, including fraud proofs, validity proofs, finality, and implementation trade-offs.

Lesson 3 - Sidechains, Appchains, and Layer 2s

Distinguishes these systems by security model, specialization, computation, and relationship to a base chain.

Covers delayed finality, fragmented liquidity, bridge risk, scripting limits, and the security assumptions of different designs.

Introduces governance and incentive tokens, transaction batching, settlement back to Layer 1, and the economic relationship between layers.

Start with a simple question: how do we handle more transactions efficiently as blockchains grow? If a network cannot process enough activity, users can experience congestion, slow confirmation, and higher costs. Scaling matters because blockchains need enough capacity to support everyday use without giving up the properties that make them useful in the first place.

No single scaling method solves everything. Scaling involves a set of design choices. Different frameworks try to improve capacity in different ways, and each one carries its own trade-offs.

Monolithic chains handle core functions such as consensus, execution, and data availability on the same layer. They usually scale by improving the performance of the native blockchain layer. A modular framework breaks away from the single-layer approach by dividing blockchain tasks across multiple layers or systems, a pattern often described as separation of concerns.

Horizontal scaling divides work across parallel systems. Sharding is one version of this idea: instead of every part of a network processing the same workload, different shards handle different portions of data or activity and coordinate their results.

Rollups represent one of blockchain’s most important scaling approaches. They process transactions away from the main chain, batch them together, and settle them on Layer 1. In the Ethereum ecosystem, this allows rollups to increase throughput while still connecting back to the base layer for security and settlement.

Key topics include two main approaches: Optimistic rollups and Zero-Knowledge rollups. Both aim to process more transactions efficiently, but they take different paths to transaction validity.

Sidechains and Layer 2s both aim to scale blockchains, but they differ fundamentally. A sidechain is an independent blockchain with its own security mechanism. It can communicate with a main chain and benefit from ecosystem effects, but it is not secured by the base chain in the same way a Layer 2 is.

Layer 2s are more tightly integrated with the base chain. They rely on a Layer 1 blockchain, such as Ethereum, for finality and consensus assumptions. Appchains offer another path by creating custom blockchains tailored for specific applications, such as gaming or DeFi.

Several hurdles still shape the adoption and efficiency of blockchain scaling. Optimistic rollups involve delayed finality because of the challenge period. Liquidity can become fragmented as assets move across ecosystems. Bridges and cross-chain communication can help connect networks, but they also introduce additional risk.

Different scaling solutions have different security considerations. Rollups inherit security from the main chain but depend on properly implemented fraud or validity proofs. Sidechains rely on their own consensus. Bridges connect ecosystems but have historically been difficult to secure. This is why scaling is not only a performance question; it is also a security and design question.

Many Layer 2 solutions introduce their own tokens for governance, incentives, or fee reductions. These tokens can encourage participation, fund network development, and reward users or service providers. Other important topics include the relationship between Layer 2s and the base layer: rollups bundle many transactions into a batch and submit that batch back to Layer 1.

Scaling is essential if blockchains are going to support broader use cases such as DeFi, NFTs, gaming, and everyday applications.

Monolithic and modular blockchains approach scaling differently, and neither model is automatically best in every context.

Rollups process transactions away from the base chain and settle them back to Layer 1.

Optimistic and ZK rollups differ in how they verify transaction validity.

Sidechains, Layer 2s, and appchains each make different trade-offs around security, specialization, and decentralization.

Bridges, fragmented liquidity, and security assumptions are central challenges in the scaling ecosystem.

Layer 1: A base blockchain that provides its own consensus, execution, and settlement environment.

Layer 2: A scaling system connected to a base chain, often used to process activity more efficiently.

Rollup: A scaling approach that batches transactions and posts data or proofs back to a base chain.

Optimistic rollup: A rollup design that assumes transactions are valid unless challenged.

ZK rollup: A rollup design that uses cryptographic validity proofs to demonstrate correctness.

Fraud proof: Evidence submitted to challenge an invalid transaction or state transition.

Validity proof: A cryptographic proof that transactions were processed correctly.

Sidechain: An independent blockchain that can communicate with another chain but uses its own security.

Appchain: A blockchain built for a specific application or use case.

Bridge: Infrastructure that moves assets or messages between chains or layers.

Fragmented liquidity: A situation where assets and liquidity are split across multiple chains or venues.

Sequencer: An entity or mechanism that orders transactions in many Layer 2 systems.

After Scaling & Layer 2s, useful next topics include Market Structure (/learn/crypto-market-structure-basics/), DeFi (/learn/defi-basics/), Ethereum & Layer 1s (/learn/ethereum-layer-1s-basics/), and the deeper Scaling & Layer 2s 201 (/layer-2-scaling-solutions/) guide.

Start the full Scaling & Layer 2s 101 course below

Layer 2 scaling refers to systems that help a base blockchain process more activity by moving some transaction work to another layer while remaining connected to the base chain.

Blockchains need scaling because limited throughput can lead to congestion, slower transactions, and higher costs when demand rises.

A rollup processes transactions away from the main chain, batches them together, and settles the batch back to Layer 1.

Optimistic rollups assume transactions are valid unless challenged, while ZK rollups use validity proofs to prove correctness upfront.

No. Sidechains are independent blockchains with their own security assumptions, while Layer 2s are more directly connected to a base chain for settlement or security assumptions.

Bridges connect different networks, but they can add smart-contract, validation, custody, or trust assumptions that users need to understand.

#5062. Elon Musk Joins 160,000 Backing Petition to Bring Jensen Huang Back to Nvidia

Elon Musk Joins 160,000 Backing Petition to Bring Jensen Huang Back to Nvidia

Elon Musk has thrown his support behind a campaign to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO, as the ousted chipmaker co-founder reportedly weighs a comeback just days after resigning.

"A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," the Tesla and SpaceX CEO tweeted on Friday. Musk had previously said it would be "an honor" to hire Huang.

A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 13, 2026

The "Stand with Jensen" open letter calls on Nvidia's board to bring Huang back while an independent investigation establishes the facts. It has drawn more than 160,000 signatures, including Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, CNBC reported, though the site notes that signatories' affiliations are self-reported and unverified. More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, The Guardian reported, a figure it said was equivalent to 18% of the company's workforce.

The campaign follows internal calls from Nvidia staff for Huang's return.

Huang has discussed the possibility of returning with confidants, the Financial Times reported, citing multiple people familiar with the matter. One ally told the newspaper they were assembling a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his reinstatement and would seek support from the White House, adding that the effort had Huang's backing.

Even supporters acknowledged the obstacles. "Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offence," one person involved in the effort told the FT.

Two major Nvidia shareholders, Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management's Gavin Baker, urged the board in an open letter on Friday to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang."

Huang resigned as Nvidia's president, CEO and board member on Thursday, capping a week of reports of affairs with Alice Huang, a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom U.S. officials suspect of spying for China, and with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO.

The campaign faces resistance in Washington. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia should look outside the company for its next CEO. "They need a dramatic shake-up," he told Fox News.

Bessent said on Sunday Morning Futures that questions over Nvidia's compliance with U.S. export restrictions were the bigger issue, and that the company should be judged on whether it had "intentionally ignored the warning signs" of shell companies in Singapore. He said he wanted answers "in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel." Huang also faces congressional inquiries into Nvidia's chip exports to China, as well as a proposed shareholder class action.

Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as a potential successor, the FT has reported. "We are in the process of selecting a search firm for the NVIDIA CEO role. We have not formally engaged any potential candidates," an Nvidia spokesperson told CNBC.

Analysts are divided on Huang's chances. "We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO," Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. said in a note cited by CNBC, while Seaport Research Partners' Jay Goldberg said Huang could stage "a second act" if he gets through his legal troubles. Former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci was blunter: "The FBI doesn't take petitions," he tweeted.

Nvidia reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, the first under Kress.

#5058. Vitalik Buterin Now ‘a Total Bull’ on leanPCS as Fast Track to Quantum-Safe Ethereum

Vitalik Buterin Now ‘a Total Bull’ on leanPCS as Fast Track to Quantum-Safe Ethereum

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has thrown his weight behind a proposal he says could make the network quantum-safe much faster than expected.

"Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull," Buterin tweeted on Monday, in a lengthy explainer on how Ethereum could handle the much larger signatures and proofs that quantum-resistant cryptography requires.

Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull. So let me explain some of these buzzwords in more detail.

At the core, 8288 is about hyper-scaling data and execution for any computation that needs to get performed on a piece of data…

— vitalik.eth (@VitalikButerin) November 16, 2026

In short, leanPCS is a proposed way for Ethereum to bundle many large, quantum-safe signatures and proofs into a single compact proof, so that the full data never has to be stored onchain. It is built on polynomial commitment schemes, or PCS, the core mathematical building block of STARK proofs.

Quantum computers are expected to eventually break the elliptic curve cryptography that secures Ethereum and Bitcoin accounts today. The quantum-safe replacements are far bulkier: Buterin said signatures would grow from 65 bytes to between 1 and 6 kilobytes, while zero-knowledge proofs would balloon from a few hundred bytes to around 128 kilobytes. "This is unsustainable to put on chain," he wrote.

Buterin's answer is EIP-8288, a draft proposal he co-authored with developer Thomas Coratger in June, which would aggregate those signatures and proofs before they ever reach a block.

Under the design, users publish their signatures or proofs, and network nodes repeatedly bundle everything they have seen into a single STARK, a type of zero-knowledge proof, that attests the underlying data is valid. These aggregate proofs are themselves combined until a single "master proof" verifies everything in a block. Only short claims, rather than the full signatures or proofs, would need to be stored onchain.

He laid out three ways to build it, depending on what users submit. The simplest, leanSPHINCS, would support a single type of quantum-safe, hash-based signature, costing users only a small amount of gas per signature, but it couldn't do anything else.

Buterin's preferred option, leanPCS, offers a third route. It would offer the same generality as leanSTARK but "could potentially be implemented very quickly," he said, because far fewer design choices are needed, and leanSTARK could then be added later.

"So there is a route to getting 'the cryptographic proof singularity' much faster than any of us expected," Buterin wrote, "and that route runs through 8288 with leanPCS."

Buterin linked to SPHINCS-, a family of hash-based signature schemes optimized for Ethereum, which was published on the Ethereum Research forum in June with input from Buterin and Ethereum Foundation cryptographers. The post shows that a standards-aligned quantum-safe signature can already be verified on Ethereum for about 150,000 gas, without any protocol change, compared with about 3,000 gas for an ECDSA signature today, according to an earlier Buterin estimate.

Under protocol-level aggregation, a future "leanSPHINCS" verification would cost about 3,000 gas, according to the post.

#5057. Tom Lee says Ethereum’s ‘waterfall decline in price’ defies fundamentals as Bitmine adds 7,653 ETH

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The Ethereum treasury company added 7,653 ETH last week, bringing its holdings to 6.08 million tokens worth approximately $11.1 billion.

Bitmine Immersion Technologies Bitmine Immersion Technologies, Inc. (BMNR) increased its Ethereum holdings to 6,077,745 ETH after acquiring 7,653 ETH over the past week, the company said in a statement on Monday.

At $1,823 per ETH, the holdings were worth approximately $11.1 billion as of Nov. 15. The position represents 4.97% of Ethereum's total supply of 122.2 million ETH, according to the statement.

Bitmine said it has staked 5,227,037 ETH worth $9.5 billion, or 86% of its position. The company projects $245 million in annualized staking revenue at current levels and up to $285 million if it staked its entire position at a 2.57% yield.

The company also disclosed several other positions, including 216 BTC, a $180 million stake in Beast Industries, a $67 million stake in Eightco Holdings, and $448 million in cash. Its combined crypto, cash, and other investments totaled $11.8 billion, down from $14.5 billion reported at the beginning of the month.

Last week, Bitmine reported a net loss exceeding $6.3 billion for the fiscal year ended Aug. 31, compared with $348.6 million in net income a year earlier. The loss came from unrealized fair-value losses on digital assets.

Bitmine Chairman Tom Lee called ETH's recent losses a "waterfall decline in price" that diverges from ongoing institutional momentum on the underlying network.

"This waterfall decline in price is not consistent with what we view as the relatively positive cadence of fundamental developments, including multiple financial institutions and banks announcing tokenization projects built on Ethereum," he said in the statement.

Lee attributed some of the pressure to margin selling in Asia tied to Nvidia and investors building cash positions ahead of Anthropic's planned Nov. 18 IPO. He said ether's recent slide closely mimics its performance before SpaceX went public in June.

The asset fell 39% in the eight weeks before that offering and 29% in the final two weeks. The corresponding declines ahead of Anthropic's IPO are 39% and 28%, according to Lee.

Ethereum traded above $1,800 on Monday, down 1.62% over 24 hours. Bitmine shares closed at $17.58 on Friday, down 4.72%.

#5055. What Does It Really Mean to Be Fit for Your Age? My Mom and I Put It to the Test at the Super Age Games

These eight fitness challenges allegedly predict how long and well you’ll live.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

What if you could predict your healthspan? That’s the idea behind the Super Age Games, which bills itself as “the world’s first live longevity fitness competition,” helping participants gauge how long they’ll live well.

The games (which took place this year in New York City on November 7) are centered around eight trials testing markers that predict longevity: grip strength, aerobic capacity, agility, balance, functional strength, memory, and relational capacity. Anyone could sign up and compete throughout the day with a thousand other athletes. There was an overall winner, a team competition winner, and winners within each age group for women and men. But also, all participants received a medal and a report outlining their strengths and areas of improvement, as well as personalized longevity training tips.

This fall, the creators behind the Super Age media brand hosted a practice day in NYC where anyone could attend and be the first to test-run the trials. My mom—who’s been interested in all things health and wellness since she was my age (I’m 26, she’s now 64). She happened to be visiting me in the city that weekend, so she signed us up.

Even as lifelong gym rats, after we experienced the tests, we both realized there are key areas of training that our workout routines are missing. Here’s what the competition taught us about our overall health—and what we can work on to live stronger for longer.

As we walked into the venue, the Metropolitan Pavilion, we noticed cones, obstacles to jump over, balance beams, and air bikes sitting on hardwood floor spread throughout the room into different stations. I felt like I was right back in elementary school taking on a field-day-meets-presidential-physical-fitness-test challenge.

There appeared to be people of all ages there—people younger than me, up to those in their 70s—and an even split between women and men. Some people came to practice day because they got the invite from being on the Super Age newsletter mailing list and wanted to try it out, while others came because they were competing at the real event in November.

My mom and I didn’t train for the specific challenges beyond our general fitness routines (a few days a week of strength training and cardio), so we weren’t sure how we would fare. However, there was time to practice each station before the actual games started—so we explored the balance beam and obstacle course.

After all of the participants arrived and everyone settled in, we were split into groups and began each trial in a specific order. We had to wait a bit to begin, and there was also a bit of downtime in between each trial as we waited for room to open up on the equipment. While the trials themselves were timed, the time in between the trials wasn’t, so we could take our time a bit and catch our breath.

The goal of each trial was different: Some were to be completed as fast as possible, or as slow as possible, while some were based on data like getting your highest VO2 max. After the practice day, we received an email of our scores, which were adjusted based on age and sex, and compared us against the other 50 athletes who participated. (During the actual Super Age Games, though, the data field was much larger.)

The email also included an action plan recommending how we could improve each of our scores. The feedback came from the work they’ve done with the Buck Institute for Research on Aging, performance coach Andy Walshe, PhD, and their head trainer, as well as longevity research and expert interviews, according to Heather Hurlock, founding editor at Super Age.

The challenge: Jump over and crawl under four gates set 10 meters apart as fast as possible to test agility, explosive movement, and gait speed, which research shows are predictors of how long you’ll live.

At first glance, my mom and I were both intimidated by the plywood box (about 2.5 feet tall) we had to jump over. It took a second to figure out how to jump over the box because everyone did it differently, but eventually, we got into the swing of things. My mom and I took off in a running start, maintained our speed throughout as we jumped over the boxes and slid under the ropes, and agreed that the challenge wasn’t that hard, and in fact, we both really enjoyed it! (However, we did end up with a few bruises from hitting the boxes and floor pretty hard.)

I finished in 80 seconds, while my mom finished in 73. (Go, mom!) Our feedback—formed from the research that Super Age has done—told us that our agility is above average.

To get better at moving quickly over and under obstacles, add in jumping exercises like directional hops and line drills, before more advanced exercises such as lateral shuffles and single-leg hop overs. These drills will help grow your coordination, balance, and power skills, as well as spatial awareness. Plus, these moves will increase your lateral quickness and help develop foot speed—all important for helping prevent falls as you grow older.

The challenge: Complete a six-minute memory game from NeuroTracker, a cognitive training tool, on computers to focus on cognitive capacity under load. Keep track of a specific set of balls moving across the screen and identify them seconds later as the speed of the balls increases.

My mom and I found that the longer the game went on, the harder it was, because we’re so used to looking at short-form content all day, so it was hard to keep focus. We couldn’t take our eyes (or mind) off of the screen for even a second, or else we were screwed for that round. (But hey, at least I know it was good for my brain.) My mom got a near-perfect score, while I had some room to grow.

Take your aerobic exercise seriously, which has been associated with improved cognitive function in older adults, suggests Aashaun Khedaru, exercise physiologist supervisor at the Sports Performance Center at NYU Langone Health. The Super Age feedback recommended walking briskly for 30 minutes, three to five times a week, to boost blood flow to the brain, and pairing it with memory or reaction games.

The challenge: Walk forward and then backward on a 12-foot balance beam carrying a 10-lb hydro training tube filled with water, front-racked, in as few steps as possible—without stepping off—to gauge balance and stability.

This trial was my personal favorite, and the one I felt most confident on (possibly due to six years of classical ballet training). There was a learning curve to just holding the tube—it could easily throw you off balance. But I just had to move slowly and keep my focus straight ahead and slightly down. I scored lower than I thought I would, though, with 49 steps, because I thought the goal was to just not fall off—not to take the smallest amount of steps possible.

For my mom, though, this one was more challenging, especially the part where we walked backward with the hydro tube. She said the level of coordination it required almost felt like trying to catch a ball while balancing on one leg. But when she engaged her core, walking the beam became easier. (She even scored better than me, finishing in 30 steps!)

The Super Age Games feedback recommended standing on one leg for 30 seconds per side each day, then trying it with our eyes closed, and adding some lunges and single-leg deadlifts into our routines. (We already do!)

Lunges can improve muscle function and balance because they isolate the quads and work your range of motion, according to a small study that had middle-aged women do eight weeks of lunge exercises to better their lower extremity strength and balance. Single-leg deadlifts can increase muscular strength and balance since it puts you in an unstable position, per a 2026 study in Scientific Reports that had 30 men perform the exercise on unstable surfaces to see if it limited joint mobility and strength gains.

The challenge: Pedal at an all-out effort on an assault bike for four minutes to earn your highest VO2 max, which is the maximum amount of oxygen your body can hold during exercise. The better your VO2 max is, the more efficiently your body produces energy, which means better endurance and stamina.

This trial carries the most weight in the overall score, Hurlock says—and the games’ creators warned it would be the toughest. My mom agreed: It was straight-up “just hard,” she said. After three grueling trials, the thought of going all out on the assault bike for four minutes was less than appealing. So, we both held back for most of it, though I kicked things into high gear for the final minute.

My score was pretty average, while my mom fared slightly better. But according to Khedaru, this four-minute challenge wasn't the most accurate way to measure VO2 max. For a more precise reading, you'd typically undergo a longer, supervised treadmill test in a lab. Fitness wearables like Apple Watches and Fitbits can also estimate VO2 max using workout data.

Your VO2 max will depend on your age and workouts, but this chart depicts where you should aim to be, based on your age:

My action plan said to do brisk walks or easy cycling to build toward HIIT, while my mom’s plan recommended adding one weekly 4x4 session to her routine: four minutes hard, then three easy, four times through. (I already run for about 90 minutes every week and do some light zone 2 work, so I feel pretty good in the cardio department.) But you can also walk or run on an incline and eventually do longer cardio sessions (45 minutes to an hour at a conversational pace) to improve your endurance. Aim for two to four cardio workouts per week.

The challenge: Crawl across a 40-foot cargo net as fast as possible to gauge functional strength and coordination.

We felt like little kids again, climbing over the net like we were back on an elementary school playground. It also tested the most aspects of longevity, in our opinion: coordination, core strength, upper-body strength, flexibility, mobility, and mental focus. I was feeling a bit lightheaded at this point in the trials (probably because it required me to be bent over crawling and I hadn’t eaten much that day), so it was harder than I thought it would be. It took my mom a second to get into a rhythm and figure out where to place her hands and feet, but once she did, she enjoyed it.

I completed the challenge in 69 seconds while my mom finished in 115 seconds (almost two minutes).

To improve functional strength and coordination, Khedaru recommends targeting the posterior chain (the backside of your body) through a mix of upper- and lower-body compound movements, which work multiple muscles. Think shoulder presses, pull-ups, lateral pulldowns, and farmer’s carries, since most of your body weight will be on your arms and shoulders. But you can also add some step-ups into your routine as well since crawling involves some leg work too; other functional leg exercises include squats, deadlifts, lunges, and calf raises, WH previously wrote. All of these exercises will build strength in your hamstrings, glutes, quads, and calves.

The challenge: Dead hang on a bar for as long as you can to test grip strength, one of the biggest predictors of longevity.

I consider myself to have a decent amount of upper-body strength, but dead hangs are still challenging. On my mom’s part, she got a shoulder replacement two years ago, so she’s had to build her shoulder strength from the ground up, particularly with hangs. (Thankfully, they let us use chalk, which can absorb sweat and moisture and make it easier to grip the bar.)

We both hung for over a minute each, which was far longer than we’d hung in practice at the gym, so we were very happy with our times. According to Khedaru, that’s good too: He says women in their 20s and 30s should be able to hang for over 70 seconds, while those in their 40s to 60s should be able to hold 45 seconds.

You can practice hanging, but also lean on farmer’s carries and kettlebell swings so your hands practice holding heavy weight and improving that grip strength.

The challenge: Complete two exercises on an iPad game to test your emotional intelligence, as research shows that those with stronger social relationships live longer. First, stare at a neutral face, then identify an emotional face that flashes on screen for two-tenths of a second (anger, contempt, surprise, happiness, etc.); eventually the faces will be shown for a shorter period, one-tenth of a second. Next, choose how you’d respond to five real-life scenarios where conflict is involved. Example: “Someone cuts in front of you with the airport line and you're going to miss your flight. Do you call them out on it or do you let it go because it's not worth it?”

The first exercise felt extremely difficult because we were already physically and mentally fatigued from the previous trials; the emotions blinked so quickly that you could barely tell which facial features had changed. So, I feel like I didn’t do as well as I wanted—especially because I was already so mentally fatigued. However, the second exercise went way better; it was pretty easy for us to pick which ones were the “correct” answers. (Honestly, it reminded me of those HR training situational videos that you have to complete for work every year.)

I didn’t get the best score on this one, which would’ve come with getting the most answers right, but my mom totally crushed it.

For stronger social skills, don’t be afraid to practice making new friends. Reach out in a way that feels natural for you—in person, text, DM—then choose an activity that sounds fun, but simple, like coffee or lunch, WH previously reported. Feel free to reach out to mutual friends first, if speaking to a stranger feels a bit intimidating.

The challenge: Run (or walk) 800 meters (nearly half a mile) carrying a sandbag weighing 10, 25, 40, or 50 pounds to test both grip strength and the cardiovascular system.

Unfortunately, we didn’t get to try this one because it was rainy and slippery outside—but we weren’t too disappointed, because we were tired. Still, Khedaru says that for 20- and 30-year-olds, your goal should be to carry 25 percent of your total body weight and complete the challenge in under 5 minutes. Those who are older should be able to carry 15 to 25 percent of their body weight and finish in around 6 minutes.

Khedaru says to regularly train your aerobic capacity and lift weights, specifically through exercises like farmer’s carries and walking lunges.

In fact, having a healthy balance of both aerobic and resistance training will help you in all of these challenges—which will translate to real-life longevity, Khedaru says. Make sure you’re regularly doing both low- and high-intensity cardiovascular work, as well as increasing reps, sets, and weight when you resistance train—a principle known as progressive overload.

The games were harder than we thought. Each activity by itself wasn’t too difficult, but by the time we completed all of them back to back and in a specific order, we were totally wiped out physically and mentally. For instance, the Over Under required a lot of energy and agility right off the bat, then we had to go right into the Synapse, which required a lot of mental focus. By the time we got to challenge number four—The Inferno—we both felt like we could’ve used a bit of a break. That’s why after The Sync, another challenge that used mental focus, we were fine to skip the last challenge, which required running with a heavy sandbag. It was clearly designed to be a total mental, emotional, and physical workout.

In fact, my hardest events were The Synapse and The Sync—and they certainly weren’t made easier after completing serious physical challenges. On the flip side, my mom crushed both of those challenges at 64, and it makes sense: She’s whip-smart, regularly works out, and stays on top of her brain health.

That said, at 26, I want to start strengthening my cognitive abilities now. While I work out regularly—and that does help my brain health some—I could probably play more brain and memory games (even when I’m tired) and scroll a little bit less on Instagram to lengthen my attention span. (Something my mom doesn’t do.)

Neither The Over Under nor The Net were our best events (especially the latter because it was one of the last events and we were tired). Both trials required mobility, agility, speed, and power in movements that we don’t really practice day to day: jumping and sliding over a high obstacle, and crawling over an unsteady net. But at 64, my mom was really happy that she could finish them (in great time, might I add!). For me, I’m a recreational runner and regularly do HIIT and speed work, so I felt good about my power and speed. But I could probably integrate more crawls and mobility work into my routine.

Ultimately, performing each of the eight challenges made us look differently at how we work out and live our day-to-day lives. Now, we have a good idea of our fitness and wellness strengths—and weaknesses—which will help inform our future workout and wellness habits.

In her 60s, my mom wants to do more agility, speed, and power work. As a kid, you run around, balance, hang, jump, and climb all the time, but as adults, you tend to stay more linear. Then, you naturally lose those skills because you’re not using them. So, completing this practice day made her want to try more of these challenges on a regular basis, instead of always taking the easy way through life.

For me, I’m much more motivated to be wary of and work on my long-term brain health and mental endurance. Maybe that looks like going for a run, and then playing brain and memory games instead of scrolling on Instagram.
