#5011. Want Studio-Style Pilates at Home? Start With These Editor-Tested Reformers

Our top picks for every kind of at-home Pilates setup, from compact machines to studio-worthy reformers.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If you’re a pilates princess, you already know what a reformer is, and you’re well acquainted with the many ways it delivers a low-impact, strength-building workout. However, if you’re a newbie, here’s a quick crash course: A reformer is a specially designed machine, originally developed by Joseph Pilates, that consists of springs for resistance, a moving carriage, a foot bar that you push or pull, and pulleys to hold onto or hook to your feet when performing pilates exercises.

“I’d describe the reformer as a machine designed to help create an understanding of your body with resistance,” says Sam Miles, owner and co-founder of Good Time Pilates in New York City. “It gives real time feedback so you can find sensation through the shortening and lengthening of your muscles. In short and easy terms: an assist to finding your muscle engagement!”

There are unique benefits to using a reformer that are hard to replicate in a pilates mat workout, or really any other type of workout. But that doesn’t mean you have to be advanced to start using one. “The modifications to increase or decrease challenge make it a truly universal machine for any body and any fitness level, which is very unique and just awesome,” Miles says. “You can rehabilitate with a reformer, strengthen muscles, stretch and find release work, it’s the best!”

Pilates reformers are available in different types: classical and contemporary. The classical reformer stays true to Joseph Pilates’ original design; the machines are made of wood, and have springs that all have the exact same resistance level. Purists are going to want to consider these machines.

Contemporary reformers are an evolutionary riff on the original and often incorporate springs of varying resistance that can be adjusted. The dimensions also usually vary a bit from the OG classical reformer design.

While it used to be that reformers were only found in Pilates studios, more and more women are investing in a reformer as an addition to their home gym setup. There are also less intense reformer models on the market that are specifically designed for at-home use, and these generally come in at a fraction of the cost of a classical or studio-grade contemporary reformer.

After testing a bunch of options, we narrowed down our picks to a variety of machines, including commercial-grade reformers and pared-down, reimagined reformers that are made specifically to take up less space and be more affordable.

After testing a handful of Pilates reformers, the contemporary-style Balanced Body Allegro 2 came out on top for its studio-quality, strong springs, durable build, and versatile foot bar. WH fitness contributor Talene Appleton has been using it two to three times a week to practice at home for almost two years, and it’s still in mint condition. Appleton says it’s built like a tank and is commercial-grade, so it’s the best you can get for your at-home gym setup.

Five springs are featured for varying tension to accommodate different levels—three high resistance (red), one medium resistance (blue), and one light resistance (yellow), while the steel, grippy foot bar glides effortlessly for 10 vertical and horizontal positions. “I was blown away by how much the additional positions of its foot bar allowed me to change up my usual Pilates sequences,” says Appleton. “This adds incredible versatility in terms of movement options that most competitors can’t beat.” While the foot bar is its best feature, Appleton notes it’s the most difficult to set up and requires two people to line it up evenly on each side.Appleton says this machine is best for advanced users, given there’s a bit of a learning curve at first. “Using a traditional reformer at home can be a bit overwhelming at first, especially if you’re used to having an instructor call the shots in terms of spring resistance, foot bar positions, moves, and all the rest,” she says. “I found myself second-guessing my setup and wondering if I was getting the most out of each exercise (or sometimes if the move I was doing was even a real exercise at all).” She credits YouTube and TikTok tutorials for guiding her along, specifically from Balanced Body and East River Pilates.While this is the best Pilates machine money can buy (with a steep price tag of $4,345 *sigh*) it’s heavy at 157 pounds. It’s also large, at eight feet long and three feet wide, so make sure you have adequate space before splurging. It’s also not the easiest to set up. “Setting this thing up was no joke—I knew I was in for a challenge when I saw the multiple massive, heavy boxes it arrived in,” Appleton says. She notes it took her and a friend two hours to assemble.

Read More: Balanced Body Allegro 2 Review

The classical Merrithew At Home SPX Reformer is next-level if you want to up your Pilates game. It features a foldable vertical tower, which can improve flexibility and target different muscle groups with more controlled movements, adding more challenge. It has five springs—four full-resistance and one with half-resistance. Given the springs mostly have the same resistance, this machine is designed for more advanced users.

The foot bar is adjustable with four positions for different heights, while the carriage is padded for comfort. Another call-out is the included reformer box, which adds height and range of motion to moves in the seated and lying position. It’s especially helpful for those with muscle tightness or who need to modify moves involving the knees.

While this is a great reformer to elevate your practice, it’s quite large at 96 inches long and 26 inches wide. It’s also heavy at 115 pounds. Like the AeroPilates Pro XP 557, this isn’t ideal for apartments. The tower structure also requires more vertical space, so if you don’t have high ceilings, our best overall is most likely your best bet.

Read More: Best Compact Home Gym Equipment

Pretty much all pilates reformers in this guide are relatively large, but the contemporary AeroPilates Reformer 4420 is foldable. If you’re an apartment dweller, this machine is your compact answer to your Pilates reformer dreams. It can be stashed under a couch, bed, or behind a door. At 69 pounds, it’s not the lightest, so having two people for setup is probably your best bet.

Like the AeroPilates Reformer 287, it uses cords, not springs, yet delivers impressive effectiveness. This model has four adjustable cords with varying resistances and color codes, unlike the 287: two standard resistances (black), one extra intensity (red), and one light resistance (yellow). So, this reformer is good for both beginners and those who are more advanced.

It also has a built-in cardio rebounder, which is essentially a mini trampoline at the foot bar, making it an especially good choice for someone looking for low-impact cardio options and variety.

The contemporary Your Reformer is studio-grade like our best overall reformer pick, and is super durable despite being a little over half the price. During a stay in Los Angeles, Appleton rented one for at-home workouts and was extremely impressed with its easily changeable five thick springs, and a carriage that glides smoothly and quietly. The springs are also color-coded: two heavy resistance (red), two medium resistance (blue), and one light resistance (yellow).

In terms of quality, it’s a direct competitor to the Allegro 2. “The straps are thick and definitely won’t fray on me, and the strap handles are comfortable to grip, even when my palms get sweaty,” Appleton says. It’s not compact enough for most apartments, but it’s slimmer to accommodate home spaces better.

Appleton is 5’5” and found the carriage to be wide and spacious, with plenty of room to move around from supine to standing to kneeling positions. It also accommodates her much taller boyfriend, who’s “20 times more passionate about a good reformer workout,” so it’s the real deal.

The AeroPilates Reformer 287 is the most affordable option we’ve come across. It’s dramatically less expensive than our best overall—it costs under $400! But that doesn’t mean it’s less effective. Its quality is still impressive, just not studio-grade. WH entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson, an avid Pilates practitioner, was surprised by how sturdy this machine is because of its bargain price, and since it comes pre-assembled (another plus).

But, she stresses it’s best for beginners since it only features three resistance cords. “I could see someone eventually progressing beyond the capabilities of this model, especially when it comes to exercises like footwork and running, which are classically done on four springs,” says Wilkinson. “It also lacks certain accessories you’d typically find with a studio machine—a box, which is typically used for exercises in the short-box series and in a long position for pulling straps and T-press, among others.”

Speaking of resistance, unlike our best overall, this reformer uses cords instead of springs. While they can be trickier to hook on and off, their weight is identical to springs Wilkinson uses on studio-grade models.The carriage glides smoothly, although Wilkinson notes the attached handles would fall and get in the way. She recommends tossing them aside instead of hanging on the built-in shoulder blocks. As for the foot bar, it’s stable but can’t be adjusted for specific exercises.Aside from mechanics, this reformer is extremely compact, weighing just 56 pounds, and measuring 42 inches when folded and 85 inches fully extended. Wilkinson lives in a one-bedroom Brooklyn apartment and has no issues stashing it away, although she finds it tricky to fold and wide when the foot bar is attached.AeroPilates says this product can fit people up to 6'4", but Wilkinson, who is 5’11”, says even her height was pushing the machine’s limits. “I imagine anyone much taller than I am would feel a bit crunched,” she says. She also says it’s narrow, and didn’t have additional breathing room.

While most full-sized pilates reformers don’t have a built-in trampoline at the foot bar, the contemporary AeroPilates Pro XP 557 is the first full-sized model we’ve seen with a rebounder, so cardio moves like single-leg pushups and slow squats can be added to the routine. This is especially useful for beginners getting into the groove. WH associate visual editor Berkeley Brooks found it stayed sturdy when executing explosive movements at fast paces, while the material of the main carriage prevented her from slipping around.

Brooks notes that the four strong springs are easily interchangeable and have varying resistances labeled by color: two low resistance (blue) and two high resistance (yellow). The foot bar is adjustable, thick, and quiet for added comfort, and can be placed in three positions to accommodate different heights without disrupting your range of motion.

The platform is also wide at 23 inches and long at 100 inches, so this model isn’t ideal for small apartments, especially since you need additional space to execute exercises.

On the upside, Brooks says it’s easy to build and aesthetically pleasing. “I love the addition of wood to the machine because it looks great in a home gym,” she adds.

The springs in a pilates reformer are an important consideration when you’re choosing your machine. “Springs provide resistance and feedback, so the type and responsiveness of springs deeply influence your experience,” says Mo Wolfe, owner and Pilates instructor of Evolution Pilates in Port Washington, New York.

The weight of springs can also depend on whether a machine is classical or contemporary. Classical style reformers have a heavier spring tension that is the same throughout, while modern models generally tend to offer springs with a variety of resistance levels. A reformer with springs is the type you’ll find in a Pilates studio.

Alternatively, resistance cords are sometimes used in the place of springs in reformer machines that are designed for personal and at-home use. They offer similar effectiveness and are more affordable.

Taking the size of your home into consideration is important before purchasing a Pilates machine. Not only do you want to make sure you have enough room for the machine itself, you also want to make sure there will be enough space to perform the full range of Pilates reformer exercises, like leg circles, that require room to move.

Some reformers are very big and bulky, such as our pro-level, best overall selection. They take up considerable real estate and they’re best for a home gym where they can become a more permanent fixture that won’t need to be moved once it’s installed.

If your workout space is multi-functional (i.e., it’s your living room) and your equipment needs to have a smaller footprint and be more portable so you can move it around or stash it away, look for a lighter, foldable option. Just make sure that you’ll have enough space to do the moves when it’s all set up.

Since reformer Pilates is a low-impact activity, and the resistance can be so fine-tuned for your fitness level, there are no hard and fast rules about how often you do a reformer session each week. Miles says it really comes down to how your body feels. “With the variety you can get from a reformer, daily use is manageable. At my studio we have challenging classes, stretch and release classes, technique-focused classes; variety is important!” She notes that most of her clients do three reformer sessions per week.

We picked the brains of Pilates instructors to understand what to look for when shopping for a reformer, then researched dozens of the top-rated models. From there, Women’s Health writers and editors (including fitness contributors Nicolette Accardi and Talene Appleton, and entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson) tested some of the best themselves to narrow down the options.

During testing, they paid close attention to spring and cord resistance level as a measure of whether or not the machines were ideal for beginners or more advanced users. The testers also considered size, durability, and ease of assembly to determine what sorts of spaces were needed for these machiness. Moves like planks, triceps presses, running (pushing off the foot bar), chest expansions, and leg circles were all completed during our testing Pilates workouts to really put these machine to the test.

*Additional reporting by Nicolette Accardi.

#5010. Banks are banning AI agents over security... and competition concerns

AI agents are set to automate everyday banking tasks — but banks aren’t ready to give up control of the customer relationship just yet.

Banks in the United Kingdom have drawn a line over how much access artificial intelligence should have to their customers’ money.

Four banks, including HSBC, Barclays, Lloyds, NatWest and Nationwide, have all moved to block or restrict third-party AI agents from accessing customer accounts, especially where they can make transactions without customer involvement.

There’s no evidence yet of AI agents accessing UK bank accounts just yet, but large lenders are worried about what happens if an automated system mismanages customers’ money — and who would be on the hook.

The banks might have other, unspoken concerns too.

Edgars Nemše, chief executive of GenLayer Foundation, an AI-focused blockchain infrastructure project, says routine banking tasks like paying bills, moving money and finding better rates could all be handed to agents.

Unfortunately for banks, this means agents would be able to seamlessly find customers a better deal elsewhere as soon as it’s published on the web.

“For plain accounts, that removes the switching costs and makes the space even more competitive,” Nemše tells Magazine.

That scenario could threaten more than just customer loyalty. In September, Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok warned about a possible “agentic bank run.”

If swarms of agents start moving household cash from low-yield checking accounts to alternatives offering higher returns en masse, that would drain banks of the low-cost funding they rely on to make loans. And the speed and scale “would be a problem for the entire financial system.”

Related: Coinbase CEO touts agentic finance as Base tops 100M AI payments

JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon has also warned against allowing external agents unrestricted access to bank accounts. “You don’t want rogue agents,” he said on an October earnings call.

Is an agentic bank run coming? Source: Apollo

Regardless of short-term moves to hold back the tide, AI agents look more and more likely to revolutionize banking within a few years.

Neeraj Makin, group head of strategy analytics at Emirates NBD, predicts agents will usher in a new era of around-the-clock banking and near-instant payments as normal by 2036.

“Forget about waiting for a payment for 24 hours or inter-country payments taking three days… all of that will be in seconds, atomic,” he says, with AI agents taking over most financial decisions.

Ferdinand Dabitz, chief executive of Augustus, an AI-native banking and payments company, sees a similar shift in how customers interact with financial institutions.

“Every consumer will have 10s and every business will have 100s of agents talking to their bank,” Dabitz says.

A human interface will still remain important for managing those agents and providing a layer of trust, “especially in commercial banking,” he says.

Related: Agents can trade 24/7 — but Yat Siu warns you could lose access at any time

Emirates NBD’s developer experience team argued in July that financial institutions should build their own frameworks for agentic AI, rather than allowing individual teams to develop agents without common controls.

Its Leap framework is designed to govern how agents authenticate with core banking systems, access sensitive data and carry out actions, with audit trails, monitoring and human oversight built in.

Emirates NBD says banks should build their own agentic frameworks. Source: Emirates NBD

However there are still major concerns around the reliability of agents to make major financial decisions on their own.

A recent Bank of England and FCA survey found that while 80% of responding firms had deployed AI agents, just 2% used agents with broad autonomy, identifying data security, third-party dependencies and risks like hallucinations among their biggest concerns.

The AI takeover likely won’t happen overnight; “it will come in steps,” Nemše says.

“Today I use an agent to review my own and my company’s finances every month and queue the payments, and I approve them. The next step is the natural one: once you trust it, you let it spend small amounts without asking.”

Routine bills, subscriptions and the agent’s own running costs would be among the first tasks to become autonomous, he says.

Dabitz says corporate treasury management could be an area delegated to agents, but says banks will need to be involved in developing these early applications.

While consumers may enjoy the upside of automating their finances, who’s on the hook when an agent makes a mistake?

Nemše says banks need to offer “delegated access as a normal feature” to avoid customers sharing logins with agents. Customers could set permissions and spending limits, and agents could make low-value transactions independently while requiring approval for larger amounts.

But existing dispute processes may struggle if agents begin making thousands of transactions on behalf of each customer. “Even a small share going wrong is a lot of disputes,” he says. “The processes for handling them were built for people making a few payments a week. That part still has to be built.”

The US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued a supervisory framework for banks’ use of what it calls “super intelligence,” including agentic systems, on Nov. 4.

OCC’s Super Intelligence: Supervisory Framework. Source: OCC

The framework is meant to help bank examiners assess how institutions use the technology, and does not introduce new binding requirements for banks. Scrutiny should reflect the potential consequences of an agent’s actions, its level of autonomy and the degree of human oversight.

So an AI system helping a bank employee draft a report would present a different risk from one authorized to move customer funds without approval, and the banks that get that balance right are likely to come out on top.

#5009. 'Tokenization Is Not the Finish Line': Jupiter to Let Users Borrow Against Bullish Shares

'Tokenization Is Not the Finish Line': Jupiter to Let Users Borrow Against Bullish Shares

Jupiter, the largest trading platform on Solana, is bringing Bullish's shares onchain as collateral, as part of a push to put tokenized assets to work.

The company will launch a dedicated, permissioned market on its lending platform, Jupiter Lend, starting with Bullish's NYSE-listed BLSH stock, Jupiter tweeted on Monday. More issuer tokens will follow, though the market won't be available in all jurisdictions, it added.

A NYSE-listed company is bringing its own shares directly to Jupiter Lend.

Today at Breakpoint, we announced our partnership with @Bullish to launch a dedicated, permissioned $BLSH market.

For the first time, Issuer Tokens can be used as collateral inside Solana’s… pic.twitter.com/rWWqwOcWmK

— Jupiter (@JupiterExchange) November 16, 2026

Unlike many tokenized stocks, which give holders a claim on a share, Bullish's issuer-sponsored token "is itself the share," Jupiter COO Kash Dhanda said in a presentation at Solana's Breakpoint conference in London.

Users will be able to borrow against them with fully onchain liquidations in an "institutional-grade lending market," and integrations with qualified custodians, he said. Bullish acquired Equiniti, one of the world's largest transfer agents, earlier this year, Dhanda noted.

Dhanda framed the announcements around what he called the "post-tokenization era." Most tokenized assets today are "parked, not productive," he said.

Of the roughly $460 billion in tokenized assets tracked by data platform RWA.xyz, only about $39.5 billion is actually onchain and can be moved off the issuer's platform, and just $3.4 billion is used in DeFi, according to DeFiLlama, Dhanda said, a "utilization gap" of 99%.

"There is this myth, and this is the thing that's misunderstood: 'If you put it on chain, they will come'," he said. "This is not the field of dreams," he added, arguing that, "Tokenization is not the finish line. It is actually the starting line."

Jupiter launched two other products alongside the Bullish market. The Jupiter Global Passport lets users verify their identity to buy permissioned assets, while keeping their information as private as possible using zero-knowledge data sharing, Dhanda said. It is live with KYC verification, with onchain credit scores and proof of wealth to follow, and the company is exploring licenses in different jurisdictions.

Jupiter Liquidity Services, meanwhile, will help asset issuers design their markets, seed initial capital, find market makers and integrate with Jupiter's routing so that their tokens are available across the platforms that use it. "You integrate once, you will be available everywhere," Dhanda said.

"Shallow credit markets don't drive liquidity on chain," he added. "If you cannot do more with your onchain asset than you can do with the off-chain version of it, you're probably not going to switch."

Jupiter says it has handled more than $500 billion in trading volume so far this year and paid out $162 million in yield. The Breakpoint announcements follow the company's launch last week of token baskets, yield vaults and a rebuilt portfolio, and come as other venues bring tokenized stocks to Solana. Trading platform Formation has notified the SEC of plans to trade tokenized U.S. stocks on the network.

Jupiter powers token swaps on The Information Exchange, Decrypt's trading platform.

#5007. Democratic senators warn SEC’s tokenized stock exemption has illicit finance gaps

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The SEC debuted its exemption in September that exempts tokenized securities venues from having to register as an exchange, opening the door for tokenized U.S. stocks.

Four Democratic senators are raising concerns about the Securities and Exchange Commission's newly unveiled innovation exemption to trade tokenized stocks, warning that it could open doors for illicit finance actors.

One of their main objections was that language in the exemption was too vague around illicit finance protections. The SEC debuted its long-awaited five-year exemption in September that exempts certain trading venues, called tokenized securities venues, from having to register as an exchange, opening the door for tokenized U.S. stocks.

However, the exemption has some gaps around illicit finance, Sens. Angela Alsobrooks, Ruben Gallego, Mark Warner and Catherine Cortez Masto said in their letter to SEC Chair Paul Atkins. For example, the exemption doesn't specify how know-your-customer and anti-money laundering apply to trading and also doesn't say if a platform needs to restrict who receives the tokens.

"As a result, a tokenized equity purchased by a verified individual could be transferred to an unverified wallet, including one held by a foreign person or illicit actor, beyond the reach of the U.S. regulatory perimeter," the lawmakers said in the letter.

The SEC declined to comment. Politico first reported on the letter.

All four Democrats had a significant role in negotiating broader legislation to regulate the digital asset industry called the Clarity Act. Following the midterm elections, Democrats will take the Senate and House, wielding control and oversight over key congressional committees that have jurisdiction over crypto. The SEC under the Trump administration, meanwhile, has moved forward with its regulatory agenda, which will likely draw oversight from Democrats in the coming year.

The four also had concerns about protections for retail investors around pricing and said issuers should be given the option to opt out of having their stocks tokenized.

In the letter to Atkins, the four senators asked Atkins to respond to questions about how the agency will enforce compliance with applicable AML standards and how it plans to verify disclosures and self-verification, among other things. The senators also asked that the SEC make its process more transparent by pursuing " any changes to the regulatory treatment of tokenized securities through a transparent rulemaking process."

"Though tokenization may well improve efficiencies in the market and broaden access, long-term success relies on investors and issuers trusting that this new regulatory regime upholds the safeguards that make the U.S.’s capital markets the envy of the world," they said.

Waxing provides immediate results, but the upkeep and the pain of simultaneously ripping out dozens of hairs from our legs are as painful as they sound. Enter at-home laser hair removal devices, which dermatologists and our hard-to-please editors swear by for their legs, bikini lines, underarms, and faces.

We’ve been testing and liking Ulike devices since 2022. From the ULike Sapphire Air+ to the Air 3, and now the featured Air 10 is the brand’s latest model worth owning.

The main complaint about this price-friendly tool is that it’s bulky, making it less ideal for travel. However, it does boast an ergonomic design for an overall comfortable hair removal experience. And since each treatment area requires a maximum of two minutes or less, you won’t have to worry about any discomfort for your wrist.

If you’re like us, then you’re probably a bit surprised that an at-home laser hair removal device can be so costly. However, we put this one to the test for nearly two months and saw major results. Based on our long-term testing experience, Epilaser’s effective tech, and the sophisticated design and feel, we knew it was deserving of a spot on this list. We adored it so much that we featured it as one of the best beauty launches of 2025 in our annual Skincare Awards package.

Our deputy visual director, Dangi McCoy, usesd this laser two to three times a week for two months on her right underarm to compare the results. She noticed the treated area regrew hair more slowly, and had half the amount of underarm hair compared to her left side. “At seven weeks, I’m still using the laser, but the regrowth has been so sparse I could count the hairs at a glance,” McCoy said in her Epilaser review.

Notably, this is the only featured device that use diode lasers for hair removal. As a quick reminder, using the wrong laser type, aka IPL, can cause burns in dark brown and deep skin tones. Thankfully, the Epilaser’s diodes prevent this from happening. The device’s unique laser wavelength bypasses the melanin that gives our skin its pigment, allowing it to safely remove hair rather than mistaking our skin for dark hair.

Epilaser is also extremely functional when you have limited outlets in your home or hotel room. During McCoy’s testing process, she found some of the cords to be cumbersome, so it was nice to have the flexibility of charging her device and using it cordless. It also allowed McCoy to remove hair from anywhere in her home, such as the couch while watching Uptown Girls.

OK, so what about the discomfort? Is splurging really worth it in this case? Turns out, yes! Epilaser maximizes hair removal results even if you have a low tolerance for discomfort. While no laser hair removal device is completely painless, McCoy only felt occasional quick pricks on her skin. The brand’s proprietary SPOT technology zaps up to 15 hairs per second, while leaving your skin untouched.

She was also impressed by how lightweight the cordless Epilaser felt in her hands. The device feels sturdy, and its ergonomic design enhances comfort during longer treatment sessions. Plus, this laser hair removal device looks absolutely gorgeous IRL—the bronze-tone trim truly elevates the luxurious appearance.

Given the laser’s smaller opening, you can even use this device on your face. It also comes with a soft-sided travel case with a short handle strap that’s easy to pack in your carry-on or rolling suitcase.

SmoothSkin's system works for anyone who wants something that's easy to use and doesn't require a lot of manual work or tinkering with buttons or various features. A patented sensor measures your skin before each flash and automatically selects the light best suited to your skin tone. This helps speed up the whole process, so full-body treatments take approximately 10 minutes.

It also includes a precision head to target smaller areas of the body—like the bikini line or even the upper lip or chin. The adaptable head also makes it easier to follow along your natural curves, like your kneecaps or underarms.

Like other great laser hair removal devices on the market, this one promises visible hair reduction in as little as four weeks and complete results by 12 weeks. It works so well that you’ll notice a difference after just one use, which is a true testament to this laser's power. SmoothSkin is on the pricey side, but justified by the fact that it offers unlimited flashes, allowing you to use this device for life. Overall, an excellent value over its lengthy lifetime. No wonder it earned 250 five-star Amazon reviews.

You've probably seen this popular laser hair removal device on your social media feeds, and our team says it really does live up to the hype. Nood’s proprietary PrecisionPulse laser makes all of the difference. The IPL flashes every 10 milliseconds, meaning it exposes your skin to less light that could accidentally cause burns.

Nood’s combination of continuous flashes and larger window make it better suited for larger areas, especially the legs. You can polish them off in 15 to 20 minutes, though it's harder to target smaller areas, like the upper lip. We also love the large digital display on this model.

It makes it very easy to toggle through the seven different intensity levels, and it's always clear which one you're working on. The price is friendlier than some other options, plus the brand offers a 90-day money-back guarantee, which makes this device a great option for anyone on the fence about at-home laser hair removal.

There are a lot of laser hair removal devices on the market, which is why you should consider a few of these pointers before investing.

IPL and diode lasers both slow hair growth and reduce the thickness of individual strands by scanning for pigment and targeting the hair follicle, says dermatologist Melanie Kingsley, MD. But, they each have their benefits and limitations.

IPL is the most commonly used type of light in at-home laser hair removal devices. This technology uses broad-spectrum light to target melanin, the pigment that gives your hair its color. The light is also unsuitable for dark and deep skin tones because it can’t distinguish between melanin-rich skin and the pigment of dark hair, says dermatologist Rachel Nazarian, MD. However, if you have a fair to olive complexion with dark hair, then you’re an ideal candidate for IPL treatments.

Until recently, all at-home laser hair removal devices were IPL lasers. But Epilaser has a game-changing laser for home use. Unlike IPL lights, which emit a broad spectrum of light ranging from 400 to 1,400 nm, diode lasers are unique because they use a more concentrated wavelength of light (around 810 nm). This precise wavelength means it can better target the hair follicles rather than accidentally burning your skin, making it more accessible for some people with darker complexions.

Both are effective, but diode lasers are slightly more versatile. That said, no matter which one you go with, you’ll need multiple treatments to maintain your hair-free results.

One of the biggest considerations is the number of flashes a device is equipped to deliver. This number indicates how long the device will last, according to Dr. Nazarian. "Many devices contain about 200,000 flashes, which is typically good for more than 15 years, although it also depends on how many areas you’re treating," she says. Other recommendations on this list, like the Smoothskin, have unlimited flashes, which means they'll theoretically last forever, but are pricier.

Extra features like multiple intensity modes—lower options for sensitive skin; higher settings for those who want to see results fast (see the Nood)—or interchangeable heads for precise treatment all over the body (hi, Braun) can increase the price. The amount you spend comes down to the features you want in your device and how long you want it to last.

One of the best ways to reduce discomfort during laser hair removal is to use cooling technology. It lowers your skin’s temperature—before, during, and after each laser pulse—to help you better tolerate longer and higher treatment settings safely.

Devices with bigger heads are more efficient on large areas. For more targeted flashes, opt for rigs with compact heads, such as the Iouniya Laser Hair Removal, which can be used on both the face and body. If you have sensitive skin, consider stretching your treatments out to once a month to start and gradually up the frequency once your skin can handle the laser hair removal treatment. The final hair-free results will take longer to achieve but at least you won’t risk irritating your skin. FWIW, she says you’ll notice thinning hair after your first four treatments.

Once you choose your device, know that it can take some time to see results. While every device is different, you’ll probably use it weekly anywhere from four to 10 weeks before noticing lasting results, says dermatologist Bertha Baum, DO. The final results might take longer to achieve, but you won’t risk irritating your skin. FWIW, warm weather likely won’t return until April or early May, meaning you’ve got several weeks to achieve smooth results. Either way, Dr. Baum says you’ll notice thinning hair after your first four treatments.

This technology has come a long way and, while pricey, it's a long-term investment that pays for itself. Think of it this way: A laser that costs $500 is basically the same price as a professional hair removal session, and that in-office treatment won't last forever, but you will continue using your at-home laser for years. And FWIW, we found a few discounted, top-rated Amazon picks that start at just $42, but you’ll want to hurry since these are fleeting deals.

At Women’s Health, we prioritize hands-on editor testing to ensure you don’t waste your time or money. Ahead is insight on what went into our editorial process while trying the latest and greatest at-home laser hair removal devices.

After testing these devices since February 2022, beauty director Brian Underwood, deputy deals and trends editor Eunice Lucero-Lee, and luxury commerce editor Sarah Maberry whittled down this list to 12 of the best laser hair removal devices. We also tapped contributors Jasmine Gomez, Lily Wohlner, and Brigitt Earley to ensure these devices work across most skin tones.

They all boast impressive features, are comfortable to use, and offer incredible value. Plus, these picks are FDA-cleared, so they’ve been evaluated for safety and efficacy. Several dermatologists also shared their no-fail laser hair removal tips and best-in-class product recommendations.

And because we know what it’s like to ball on a budget, we also considered pricing. TBH, laser hair removal devices aren’t exactly cheap. Many cost between $300 and $600, especially when shopping for these expert-approved devices from well-respected brands, such as Braun.

To help, I carefully researched dozens of other cheaper, yet top-rated Amazon laser hair removal devices. Ultimately, I found four Amazon picks that are aligned with expert guidance and are currently discounted as low as $35. Talk about major savings! For added peace of mind, they all earned thousands of rave reviews from real Amazon customers.

So if you're ready to ditch daily shaving and bi-monthly waxing, we're confident—based on our own testing and our dermatologists' advice—that this list contains only the best, most effective options on the market worth your hard-earned coins.

Dr. Nazarian confirms at-home laser hair removal devices are generally safe and effective, citing a 2019 paper. The biggest challenge with many at-home devices comes down to their inability to differentiate between dark skin and dark hair due to their pigmentation. Melanin-rich complexions risk absorbing too much laser energy that increases the risk for burning, cautions Dr. Nazarian. If this is you, then see your dermatologist for a recommendation on the best laser hair removal treatments and devices.

It's also a good idea to do a patch test and not expose the treated area to sunlight for a week, says Dr. Shirazi. Your treated skin is temporarily more sensitive, and you risk sunburn, hyperpigmentation, and delayed healing. She also doesn’t suggest using the laser on tanned and tattooed skin, open wounds, moles, or birthmarks to avoid changing their appearance or causing accidental burns.

Truthfully, they're not optimal for sensitive or dark skin. Many at-home devices cannot distinguish between melanin-rich complexions and dark hair, says dermatologist Corey L. Hartman, MD. Anyone else can still give them a try.

And, like with salon treatments, it's important to practice patience—this isn't a "one and done" situation. Many devices need to be used multiple times weekly to achieve the initial results. Plus, each at-home session can take 10 to 60 minutes, depending on how much body and facial hair you plan to remove. While a tad annoying upfront, this minor inconvenience has a major payoff because your hair will regrow slower over time with regular use.

#5003. Trezor hit by another shipping partner data leak, affecting 27,000 Skladon orders

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The breach exposed names, addresses and purchase details, following a similar leak at ShipMonk in August.

Trezor customer names, addresses, and other personal information were leaked in a breach at shipping partner Skladon, affecting roughly 27,000 orders. It's the second such incident for the crypto wallet manufacturer since August.

In a Sunday announcement, Trezor said Skaldon notified the company that its systems holding customer shipping data had been accessed by unauthorized parties. The breach reportedly occurred on Nov. 7, with the attacker believed to have exported information on orders placed between Aug. 9 and Nov. 7.

The stolen information included "full names, phone numbers, delivery addresses, email addresses and order details." Trezor reassured users that its own systems were unaffected and that no wallet backups, PINs, or passphrases were leaked.

The report said that some customers were already reporting that they received scam calls from bad actors using that data to impersonate support staff.

"Please be alert to potential risks to your physical security," Trezor warned.

The incident follows an August breach at ShipMonk, another of Trezor's shipping partners, which exposed personal information on approximately 13,700 customers across seven countries. Most had their phone numbers and shipping addresses exposed.

"We know this is not the first time customer contact details and addresses have been exposed in an incident involving one of our partners," Trezor said.

The company said it is reviewing its third-party partners and working to cut the time it holds order data from 90 days to 45 days.

It also introduced anonymous pickup in 18 European countries, letting customers pick up their orders without giving their names or home addresses. Trezor said it is working on rolling out the feature to U.S. customers "as soon as possible."

#5002. Saylor’s Strategy Keeps Buying Bitcoin, Adding 'A Little Orange' Through the Dip

Saylor’s Strategy Keeps Buying Bitcoin, Adding 'A Little Orange' Through the Dip

Strategy kept buying Bitcoin through a brutal market stretch, adding 485 BTC worth roughly $33.4 million and repurchasing $228 million of its preferred stock, as chairman Michael Saylor urged the market to rally with a characteristically cheeky nudge.

The company disclosed the purchase in a filing Monday. The modest addition, small by the standards of a firm that once bought tens of thousands of coins at a time, lifted Strategy’s total holdings to 850,849 BTC as of Nov. 15, alongside $4.9 billion in U.S. dollar assets.

Strategy, the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, remains far ahead of any other treasury company.

The buy caps a stretch of smaller, steadier accumulation paired with stock buybacks. Strategy recently added $82 million in Bitcoin while repurchasing $188 million of its STRC preferred shares, part of a shift toward what it calls a capital-management approach, buying back stock when it views the shares as undervalued rather than relentlessly stacking coins.

Bitcoin has slid sharply in recent days, trading well below the six-figure highs it touched earlier in the cycle, and the downturn has squeezed Bitcoin treasury firms whose valuations rise and fall with the asset.

Saylor, undeterred, posted the holdings update to X alongside the firm’s trademark Bitcoin tracker, and followed it with a quip aimed at the slumping market: “This dip could use a little orange,” a nod to Bitcoin’s signature color.

The purchase lands during a precarious moment for the treasury-company model Strategy pioneered. Index provider MSCI has finalized rules that could eject Bitcoin treasury firms like Strategy from its widely tracked equity indexes, classifying companies whose balance sheets are dominated by a single asset as “non-operating” and therefore ineligible.

Removal would force index-tracking funds to sell the affected shares, potentially pressuring prices and shrinking the premium these firms have long commanded over the value of their Bitcoin.

For now, Strategy is doing what it has always done, buying Bitcoin and talking it up, even as the market tests its conviction.

The combination of a small purchase and a sizable buyback underscores the balancing act: keep accumulating, defend the stock, and weather a downturn that has turned the once-unstoppable treasury trade into a far more fraught proposition.

#4999. CFTC backs blockchain-based derivatives infrastructure as Backpack, tZERO win approvals

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

On Monday, CFTC Chair Michael Selig said the agency had approved the applications, marking another sign of its increasingly crypto-friendly regulatory approach.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has approved applications from Backpack and tZERO to establish regulated derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses that use blockchain technology to execute and settle transactions.

On Monday, CFTC Chair Michael Selig highlighted the approval of a blockchain-based derivatives exchange and clearinghouse, which appears to correspond to Backpack's newly announced U.S. regulatory approvals.

"These approvals mark an important milestone in the evolution of American financial markets and demonstrate that there is a regulated pathway for a new generation of market infrastructure built using blockchain technology," Selig said.

Financial tech company tZERO received its exchange approval last week, following its earlier approval from the agency to operate a derivatives clearing organization, which it says will allow the firm to "support derivatives trading and clearing through its own regulated entities."

"The approvals establish a unique new derivatives market infrastructure vertical within tZERO's growing Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) business, enabling the company to develop exchange and clearing services for financial institutions and other market participants," tZERO said.

Backpack announced its approval from the CFTC on Monday. In a statement, Backpack US President Mark Wetjen called the approvals a "really big deal."

"This is an achievement that demonstrates that the highest standards of regulatory compliance and blockchain innovation can go hand in hand," Wetjen said.

Over the past year, the CFTC under Selig has taken significant steps for crypto regulation, including working with the Securities and Exchange Commission to clarify which digital assets are securities or commodities, creating an innovation task force and supporting 24/7 trading and bitcoin perpetuals.

Selig, who currently serves as the CFTC's sole sitting commissioner, could soon have fellow commissioners. Last week, President Donald Trump tapped Nathan Anonick and Matthew Rowland to be commissioners at the CFTC. The Senate Agriculture Committee will hold its nomination hearing for the bipartisan pair on Tuesday, after which their nominations could head to a full Senate confirmation vote.

Before buying a winter coat, think about where you’ll be using it. Are you living in a big city or a rural area? Does it get crazy cold or more temperate in the winter? How active are you? Once you've decided what you need, you can get into the nitty-gritty of coat shopping.

The key to a warm winter coat? Insulation. But there are two main types to consider: down and synthetic. Learning a bit about them can guide you in choosing the right coat for your lifestyle.

The bottom line: If you live in a wet environment and want to spend less money, go with synthetic insulation. If you live in a drier, colder place and are willing to splurge a bit more, opt for a coat that has down insulation.

You want to make sure your winter jacket is warm enough to last through many seasons. And, in order to do that, you want to make sure the materials your jacket is made of are super weather-resistant, especially if you’re in an area with harsh conditions and need extra warmth and protection. Over the years, I’ve removed jackets that didn’t stand up to the test of time and added new impressive options.

#4996. Lighter recovers $5M after $10M exploit linked to compromised API keys

Lighter restored withdrawals after recovering approximately $5 million in USDC, while blockchain analysts traced $10.4 million in funds moved during the exploit.

Update 20:40 UTC: This article has been updated with details of Lighter’s $5 million fund recovery, the restoration of withdrawals and the cause of the exploit.

Decentralized derivatives exchange Lighter said it had restored withdrawals and recovered approximately $5 million after an attacker exploited compromised trader API keys in an incident involving more than $10 million in withdrawals Monday.

Blockchain analytics firm Bubblemaps said about $10.4 million in USDC had been withdrawn from the platform. It tracked funds being swapped into Ether (ETH) and Wrapped Monero XMR1, a token traded on Hyperliquid.

Lighter initially said its protocol and smart contracts were unaffected. The exchange activated Guardian mode, temporarily pausing withdrawals and new pool creation while its Security Council worked to secure the platform.

The security incident follows a string of high-profile cryptocurrency exploits this year, including the $6.3 billion Binance hack on Oct. 29, the industry’s largest to date.

Lighter and Bubblemaps identified wallet ‘0xb3f’ as the attacker’s address. Blockchain data platform Bitquery separately traced 10,393,057 USDC leaving Lighter’s Ethereum contract at 10:11 am UTC. It said most of those funds were converted into Ether through CoW Swap within minutes, followed by a series of 160 ETH transfers to wallets linked to XMR1 purchases on Hyperliquid.

Related: DOJ moves to seize $1.2B from Binance hack, disrupts FaceStealer scam

In subsequent analysis, Bitquery identified a total of 1,920 ETH transferred through 12 wallets, each receiving 160 ETH (about $290,000) before routing the funds through LI.FI toward Hyperliquid.

The 12 Hyperliquid accounts purchased approximately $3.46 million in XMR1 tokens. Another 3,845 ETH, worth about $7 million, remained in the original wallet as of 11:55 UTC on Monday, according to Bitquery’s latest snapshot.

Bitquery also identified similar fund movements following a separate $6.45 million Safe wallet theft at 11:35 UTC on Monday, about 84 minutes after the Lighter withdrawal, as well as a Kava exploit two days earlier.

All three involved funds routed through LI.FI into XMR1 purchases on Hyperliquid, but Bitquery found no direct transfers linking either of the other incidents to Lighter. The firm cautioned that similar transaction routes alone are weak evidence of a common attacker.

In a postmortem published Monday at 18:20 UTC, Lighter detailed how the attacker obtained private API keys through a trader’s custom signing software, which reused cryptographic nonces, allowing the keys to be calculated from publicly available signatures.

The attacker used the compromised keys to create a public pool, transfer funds into it and withdraw them through an attacker-controlled account.

Lighter said its Guardian security mechanism temporarily paused withdrawals, allowing its Security Council to return approximately $5 million in USDC to the affected trader. The exchange said its protocol, smart contracts and official software development kits were unaffected.

Lighter has since required wallet signatures for transfers to public pools and made API-key signatures non-public. It also plans to introduce IP allowlists and configurable permissions for API keys.

#4994. Nvidia Stock Has a 20% Rebound in Sight—If Bulls Can Clear a Hurdle

Nvidia Stock Has a 20% Rebound in Sight—If Bulls Can Clear a Hurdle

If you were looking to buy Nvidia stock at a discount, last week may have been the best time to shop. Shares tanked following the Jensen Huang scandal involving an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, falling as low as $148.80.

On that drop, Nvidia shares touched a major support and then bounced after dropping 38% from its all-time high.

But if you didn’t buy the bottom, the second best time may be this week. The stock is trading at around $159, already up 8% from the lowest point last week. For traders relying on reading the charts, the current price of NVDA is running into another level that could decide whether the recovery has legs.

At around $159 on Monday, its weekly chart now places the $164.40 zone directly in the bulls' way.

That level previously acted as support, a price where buyers stepped in. After the breakdown, it is turning into a level to watch as investors who bought earlier may look to sell once they get their money back. But it could mark a bounce point based on the longer timeframes—as it has for at least three times since September 2025.

If Nvidia can reclaim $165 and hold above it, the next prominent resistance on the chart sits around $188 to $190. That would represent almost 20% upside from Monday's $159 price, although only about 16% from the breakout level, with possible selling pressure along the way.

Failure to clear $164.40 would put $152.62 back on the radar. Another break below that yellow support would weaken the case that last week's bounce marked a bottom.

The exponential moving averages, or EMAs, still offer some encouragement. Nvidia's 50-week EMA remains above its 200-week EMA, a bullish long-term configuration that gives more weight to recent prices but hasn't yet flipped bearish.

The shorter-term signals look less friendly. The Average Directional Index, or ADX, is around 23, suggesting a weakened trend (which is natural after the FUD episode). Its directional readings favor sellers. ADX measures trend strength, not direction by itself.

The Relative Strength Index, or RSI, is near 31.6, barely above the conventional oversold threshold of 30. That can make a relief bounce more plausible, but oversold stocks can keep falling. Neither indicator confirms a reversal yet.

Nvidia's underlying business hasn't suddenly stopped growing. The chipmaker reported $96.2 billion in quarterly revenue in August, up 106% year over year, including $89 billion from its data center business.

Investors will also be watching profit margins and the enormous financing commitments tying Nvidia to the wider AI infrastructure boom.

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 amid reports of extramarital affairs involving Alice Huang, a businesswoman U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China, and Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell. Reuters subsequently reported a third alleged relationship with another employee.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while an independent investigation into possible foreign-intelligence targeting continues. The espionage allegations have not been established by an independent investigation, much less in court, but were powerful enough to oust the man who led Nvidia for 33 years in record time.

The Financial Times reported that Huang has spoken with allies about returning, while a petition calling for his reinstatement has attracted more than 178,000 signatures, including Elon Musk. The board has not announced plans to bring him back.

The argument sounds familiar: Huang may be too important to Nvidia to keep out. Sam Altman returned to OpenAI days after being ousted in 2023.

Other cases of CEOs too big to let go have been Steve Jobs with Apple, Jack Dorsey with Twitter and Starbuck’s Howard Schultz. Many of these leaders have turned into the face of their companies, making it hard for the markets to trust in any successor.

For bulls, $164.40 remains the line to beat, and charts point to this outcome being quite possible. Assuming, of course, Nvidia's next big reveal is about chips and not a fourth love affair.

#4989. Fed Is Modeling AI 'Super Intelligence' Scenarios, Including Job Losses and a Stock Market Slump

Fed Is Modeling AI 'Super Intelligence' Scenarios, Including Job Losses and a Stock Market Slump

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said Monday that central bank staff have started modeling how artificial intelligence could reshape the U.S. economy, including scenarios where the technology raises unemployment even as the economy grows.

Speaking at the Fed's Productivity and Jobs conference in San Francisco, Warsh described three possible paths: a productivity boom benefiting workers, a boom that leaves workers behind, and an AI investment bust that drags down stocks and economic growth.

“These are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts,” Warsh said, explaining that staff are using simplified economic models to test what might happen over the next several years. The Fed is preparing for different outcomes, not predicting which one will materialize.

Warsh called the technology “super intelligence,” or SI. That language is now official Fed terminology after an October change following a Donald Trump administration executive order, rather than a scientific determination that today's AI systems have already surpassed human intelligence.

In the most optimistic scenario, AI helps companies produce more with the same resources, raising the country's economic output above its historical growth rate. Workers share in those gains, and unemployment stays close to the level economists associate with a healthy job market.

In the second scenario, AI still makes the economy grow faster, but businesses automate jobs more quickly than displaced workers can find new ones. Unemployment rises despite the productivity gains.

The third scenario assumes AI investments fail to deliver the returns Wall Street expects. Companies spend heavily on infrastructure, stock prices rise on expectations of huge profits, and those expectations eventually prove too optimistic.

“Equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown,” Warsh said. In that scenario, unemployment rises more sharply, and the economy eventually recovers without the promised productivity boost.

Those risks are already receiving attention elsewhere at the Fed. Governor Michael Barr warned Monday that the AI construction boom is increasingly financed through complex arrangements, including long-term computing leases, energy contracts and financial guarantees.

The Fed estimates that the potential maximum value of these off-balance-sheet obligations now exceeds $3 trillion. Those commitments are not the same as debt already owed, but they show why disappointing AI revenues could create problems beyond the technology companies building data centers.

Warsh did not propose an interest-rate change in Monday's remarks. The Fed's next policy meeting is scheduled for December 8 and 9.

#4984. Zelle picks Solana for ZelleUSD stablecoin and international payments

Zelle plans to use Solana for its ZelleUSD stablecoin and international payments, with confidential transfers designed to hide payment amounts.

Zelle, the US peer-to-peer payments network operated by Early Warning Services (EWS), a consortium of banks that includes JPMorgan and Wells Fargo, is partnering with Solana to support its expansion into international payments. The company announced on stage at Breakpoint 2026 that its proprietary dollar-backed stablecoin, ZelleUSD (ZLUSD), will launch on the Solana blockchain to allow for peer-to-peer payments internationally.

The move brings one of the largest domestic payments networks in the US into the blockchain-based payments market. Zelle processed more than $1.2 trillion in US payments in 2025 and has since taken steps to establish an international business. In June, the company named India as its first international remittance corridor, with plans to allow US consumers to send money to friends and family in the country. In the same announcement, the company unveiled ZelleUSD, intended to underpin future international payment capabilities in additional markets. ZelleUSD’s issuer is Anchorage Digital Bank.

“Sending money around the world is a pain; it’s complex, it’s fragmented and it’s often unfamiliar. Over half of the Remittance services that are offered today don’t deliver money as fast as we’d like them to,” said Alexandra Lang, vice president of digital asset partnerships at Zelle. “Solana is a partner we chose because we’re here to deliver payments at scale.”

For Zelle, the decision to select Solana appears to have been driven in large part by the network’s infrastructure. “Zelle has such a massive scale in the United States, we needed a partner that can also deliver at massive scale internationally as well,” said Denise Leonhard, General Manager at Zelle in a video discussing the partnership.

“The number one priority is the responsibility that we have to make sure that payments are safe, secure, and they get to the right place [...] That piece around trust, security, proven infrastructure is the reason why we chose Solana.”

Following several years in which network outages raised questions about Solana’s suitability for financial applications, the chain has maintained 100% uptime since February 2024. This is despite a routing failure at infrastructure provider Teraswitch in August 2026, which took 29% of Solana’s network offline. According to blockchain intelligence platform Metrika, transaction finality slowed, but uptime was sustained.

On stage at Breakpoint 2026, the Solana Foundation announced the migration of Solana from beta into mainnet, bringing with it an improvement in finality speed from 13 seconds to 150 milliseconds.

Related: HKMA, Swift explore tokenized deposits for cross-border bank payments

In the payments wallet, customers will have the option to encrypt their transfer so it is shielded from the public blockchain. Institutions that are part of Zelle’s network will be able to decrypt the transfer to carry out the checks needed to maintain compliance.

“Features like this are paramount to really getting payments to scale,” said Lang.

Related: DBS, JPMorgan’s Kinexys launch 24/7 transfers of tokenized deposits

Although Solana is gaining ground in stablecoin activity, Ethereum and Tron continue to hold substantially larger pools of dollar-pegged assets. According to Token Terminal data pulled on Nov. 14, Ethereum held $150.5 billion in stablecoins while Tron held $93.2 billion, compared with $13.9 billion on Solana.

However, Solana’s stablecoin activity is growing faster in transaction frequency than on either of its larger competitors. The network recorded an 82% increase in monthly stablecoin transfers year-over-year in October, compared with 48% growth on Ethereum, while Tron’s transfer count declined by nearly 8%, according to Token Terminal data.

Zelle’s choice of Solana over both Tron and Ethereum follows other remittance providers that have expanded on-chain. Also at Breakpoint, MoneyGram outlined an integration with Solflare allowing Solflare wallet users to exchange UDSC to cash. The move expands MoneyGram Ramps on Solana, launched by the company in August.

“That’s where MoneyGram brings something different to the ecosystem: the ability to bridge digital dollars and physical cash at scale, making stablecoins more useful in everyday life,” said Luke Tuttle, Chief Product and Technology Officer at MoneyGram in a press release.

While Zelle did not provide a timeline for the launch of international payments on stage, earlier announcements indicated that the India corridor would be live by the end of 2026.

#4981. Trump Backs Jensen Huang’s Return to Nvidia as Sam Altman Says 'Heroes Have Flaws'

Trump Backs Jensen Huang’s Return to Nvidia as Sam Altman Says 'Heroes Have Flaws'

President Donald Trump joined Elon Musk on Monday in supporting Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO, while OpenAI chief Sam Altman expressed empathy for the ousted co-founder without endorsing his reinstatement.

“I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump told reporters Monday as he left the White House for Asia, according to Reuters. “He could return. There’s a big group of people that would like him to return.”

Trump said Huang had “learned a big lesson,” and questioned claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. “Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” he said, per The Guardian.

Trump also dismissed concerns that his ties with Huang threatened national security and defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick amid questions over enforcement of AI-chip export controls.

Musk also said Friday he was signing a petition demanding Huang’s reinstatement.

“A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too,” Musk wrote on X. Epic Games boss Tim Sweeney and Replit CEO Amjad Masad are also listed among the supporters.

More than 182,000 people had signed the open letter by Monday. It seeks Huang’s return during an independent investigation, although signatories’ identities and affiliations are not independently verified.

Speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference Monday, Altman said Huang had “long been a hero of mine. Heroes have flaws.” He described feeling “personal strong empathy” for the former Nvidia boss.

He has reason to understand a boardroom revolt. OpenAI fired Altman in November 2023, only to reinstate him less than five days later after employee and investor backlash. Still, asked whether Huang should return, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.”

Altman said he struggled to imagine Nvidia without Huang, but argued the giant chipmaker was big enough to retain investor trust. That is sympathy—not an endorsement.

Huang, who founded Nvidia in 1993, stepped down Thursday after admitting infidelity. Reports later linked him to Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees, one a subordinate.

Alice Huang previously worked at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer facing scrutiny over possible diversion of advanced chips to China. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing; espionage allegations remain unproven.

Washington is tightening export controls on advanced AI chips, including new licensing requirements for shipments to Singapore and Malaysia, as officials seek to prevent diversion to China.

Trump’s backing also puts him at odds with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who said Sunday that Nvidia should look outside its ranks for a replacement. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent told Fox News.

Nvidia’s board has made no decision to reinstate Huang. CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO, while the Financial Times reports Huang’s allies are lobbying for his return and Arm CEO Rene Haas is a potential successor.

Employees have also pushed for reinstatement. An internal discussion drew more than 1,600 comments, including calls for Huang’s return.

Nvidia shares opened 2.7% lower Monday, wiping out roughly $100 billion in market value at the open.

Huang could face congressional questions on China chip exports in early December. Nvidia reports earnings Tuesday, its first financial update under Kress.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Get the chrome dome of your dreams with these scalp shavers.

AS MEN, THE decision to go bald isn’t always one that’s made for us (thanks, genetics). But how you deal with hair loss is entirely in your hands. Sure, there are some viable hair loss treatments and shampoos for thinning hair that we certainly back. For many men, it's easier to just bite the bullet and shave their hair completely to offset any future thinning woes. If you are one of these men, more power to you! Hell, some men do it even if they’re not experiencing hair loss—and that’s cool, too. Investing in a quality head shaver will double down on the convenience factor of being bald by making the entire process seamless.

When you do choose to shave your head, the tools you use to do it are paramount. That’s where the best head shavers come in. These high-tech gadgets are specifically designed to make shaving your head easier, whether it’s through a multi-head ergonomic design or close-cutting technology (or both).

Far easier than heading to the barbershop every few days, these electric shavers are meant to be used at home. Think of them as an easier, safer, and quicker alternative to carefully taking a razor to your dome. But before investing in a shaver, there are a few key factors to keep in mind to ensure you select the absolute best one for you.

This tiny but powerful shaver is designed to give your scalp the closest shave possible, whether you prefer to do it dry, wet, or with the aid of other products. Its portable design makes it easy to carry in your luggage, though its travel case is sold separately. Not to mention, the five heads of this shaver definitely give an incredibly close shave—as close as the Remington and the Braun, both of which we found to be top of the heap in our testing process.

We also appreciate the additional attachments that this one comes with, unlike the Remington, particularly the pre-shave exfoliating brush, which not only helps give a closer shave, but also feels pretty damn good on your dome (you’ll want to only use this if you have a tiny bit of stubble though—the bristles aren’t long enough to reach through longer hair).

In theory, the trimmer attachment and the accompanying guards are great if you want to trim your beard (the brand also says you can use it to trim your body and other areas), but we found that the design of the device makes that difficult. Since it’s meant to be held in the palm of your hand, it’s not as easy to use on your face as a more traditional razor design like the Braun or even the Andis. We would probably skip that and relegate this device to only our heads, which, at a comparable price point to other models like the Remington, is OK.

Read More: How to Give Yourself a Buzzcut

If you’re in a rush, this easy-to-use shaver may be your answer. Thanks to the pivoting shaver heads that hug each curve of your head, the brand says that this device can shave your entire head in just two minutes.

After testing the Remington Balder Pro for over a year, we can safely say that it easily gave us a head shave in less than five minutes, which is great for guys who cut their dome weekly. During our trial run, we found out that the fast-speed device can cut up to 40,000 cuts per minute. Thanks to its waterproof capability, you can use it in the shower for a refreshing shaving experience. We also love that the device comes with a SmartCare center, which maintains the quality for longer use and makes cleaning up a breeze.

While this isn’t technically a head shaver in the way the two Remingtons or Freebird are, we found in our testing that it performs just as well at shaving your head as it does at shaving your face—it is our best electric razor.

What that means to us is that if you’re looking to streamline the number of devices you have in your arsenal, but don’t want to sacrifice power or efficacy, this is an ideal option. This is definitely a classic for a reason—it really gets the job done with an incredibly smooth shave. However, it’s aggressive and not the gentlest experience, especially if you’re just beginning with it. Theoretically, you can use this on your face and other areas, too, but we found that the shaving experience is too harsh for us to use anywhere but our head and neck. You’ll also likely want to finish with some sort of lotion or moisturizer to minimize potential irritation.

Manscaped is one of the most consistent brands in men’s grooming, and this head shaver is a perfect example of why. It simply gets the basics right for a more enjoyable, less irritating shave. The grip, which invites palming, is super user-friendly, making moving the blades along your head easy with minimal effort (or risk of dropping it).

The brand’s signature SkinSafe blade guards make cuts and nicks rare, while the magnetic connection makes clean-up and replacements easy. With a 9,500 RPM motor, it shaves smoothly and efficiently. We found it also required minimal passes to get a full shave. Adding to its user-friendliness, the Dome Shaver Pro battery lasts up to 90 minutes and is USB-C chargeable. This head shaver from the always reliable Philips Norelco is a great choice if you’re looking for a smooth, comfortable shave without the hassle. Its 360-degree flexing head follows the contours of your scalp, while the 36 self-sharpening ComfortCut blades deliver an even shave without putting unnecessary pressure on your skin.

The ergonomic grip makes it easy to maneuver, while the PowerAdapt Sensor automatically adjusts power to match hair density as you go. With up to 90 minutes of cordless use, water resistance, and a convenient travel case, it’s a reliable option for both everyday grooming and travel.

Most head shavers feature multiple razor heads to help hug the contours of your head so you can easily navigate areas that are hard to see. The multiple razor heads can also help limit cuts, as the design adjusts to curved angles much better than a single, straight razor.

For the quickest, most adaptable (read: lowest maintenance) shaving experience, look for devices with shaving heads in the five-to-seven range, like the Freebird FlexSeries or Remington Balder Pro. That being said, don’t fall into the common trap of thinking that more shaving heads automatically equals a more powerful shave, as the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus is one of the most powerful options on the market and only has four shaving blades.

Most head shavers on this list can be used dry, which means as long as your hair is already short enough (no more than a couple of days of growth), you can shave with no moisture or product. What's also great is that some options are waterproof, making your shaving experience in the shower a total breeze and easy to clean up.

Plus, you can use most wet/dry shavers with shaving products, so if you prefer to begin with a pre-shave oil to protect your scalp and then add a shaving cream or lotion to help with gliding. Follow it up by rinsing the product off your head—just make sure to also clean any leftover product from the razor heads before you put it away. However, there are a couple of options we recommend that do not have this capability, so if you’re a dedicated shower shaver, focus solely on the wet/dry devices.

A good cordless head shaver can last as long as 90 minutes, which means you can go a whole week without charging the battery. They also unlock the ability to shave in the shower or on the road without having to be plugged in. If you're constantly on the move and shave your head regularly, you will find that cordless options offer lots of convenience and save even more time.

Even before joining the bald brotherhood, most of us have all had an electric razor or beard trimmer die out before we've finished the job. Nobody wants to sport a half-trimmed beard or uneven body hair, but the absolute last spot you'll want an uneven shave is on your dome, as it's the hardest to hide.

To avoid walking around with a patchy skull, keep battery life in mind when choosing an electric shaver. Consider how long you typically take to shave your entire head—and how often you tend to charge devices—before finalizing your decision.

The first question to ask is: Does this shaver come with a case included? If yes, then you're going to want to look at what type of case it is. For frequent travelers, a carrying case made to fit neatly in a Dopp kit or luggage should be a priority. However, if you're just looking for something to store it in, you can allow for more size, given that it'll more easily hold every attachment or replacement piece, so there won't be any long search involved when needed.

For the past four years, Men's Health's grooming writers and editors have tested over 15 head shavers to determine the best-performing options for men. We also spoke with the barber and owner of Faheem’s Hands of Precision in Philadelphia, Faheem Alexander, who has put dozens of top-selling head shavers to the test and evaluated their effectiveness, durability, and ease of use.

In addition to all of this expertise and hands-on experience, we researched and dug into the top head shavers on the market to determine which to test. Following that extensive research and testing process, we landed on these seven best head shavers for men.
