#4929. Bitmine edges toward 5% of ETH supply as treasuries report buys amid market slump

Strategy, Strive, Bitmine and Cypherpunk disclosed fresh additions to their crypto treasuries, spanning Bitcoin, Ether and Zcash.

Publicly traded crypto treasury companies Bitmine, Strive and Cypherpunk Technologies disclosed increases in their cryptocurrency holdings on Monday, joining Strategy in accumulating digital assets despite a broader market downturn.

Bitmine, the largest publicly traded Ether treasury company, said it added 7,653 Ether (ETH) over the past week, bringing its total holdings to 6.08 million ETH, about 4.97% of its total supply and bringing it ever closer to its stated aim of accumulating 5% of the ETH supply, according to a Monday announcement.

Top Bitcoin treasury companies Strategy and Strive also reported purchases. Strategy acquired 485 Bitcoin (BTC) for $33.4 million, while Strive bought 251 BTC for $17.5 million, bringing its holdings to 43,404 BTC — just 110 BTC behind Twenty One Capital, the third-largest publicly traded Bitcoin holder, according to BitcoinTreasuries.net data.

Zcash (ZEC) treasury and mining company Cypherpunk Technologies reported buying 3,775.72 ZEC for $3.48 million since September and mining another 5,721.35 ZEC in October. The additions brought its holdings to 341,858.75 ZEC, or around 2% of circulating supply.

The purchases come amid a broader cryptocurrency sell-off. Bitcoin was trading around $65,017, down 12.9% over the past seven days and 20% over the past month. ETH fell 14.2% and ZEC dropped 22.9% over the past week, according to CoinGecko data as of 8:08 pm UTC on Monday.

Bitcoin is down around 20% over the past month. Source: CoinGecko

#4928. Jenna Dewan Faced Criticism, a Partner Suspension, and a Shock Dancing with the Stars Exit. She’s Still Proud.

In an exclusive interview with Women’s Health, the actor reflects on her time in the ballroom.

Dancing with the Stars fans let out a collective gasp Tuesday night. Jenna Dewan and her partner, Val Chmerkovskiy, had earned one of the night’s top scores: 28 out of 30. They also won their dance-off against Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik, tying for second on the leaderboard with Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov. Then host Alfonso Ribeiro called Dewan’s name, eliminating her from competition.

“I had a great time, and I loved getting to share that with the world,” she said, moments after being eliminated. “All love.”

Not even 48 hours later, Jenna sat down with Women’s Health to share her story.

Jenna Dewan: Overall, it’s really been the saying, “Two things can be true at once.” There's so many different emotions, and it's kind of hard to even put into words because obviously doing a show like this is such an enormous undertaking, and it's physically, emotionally, mentally, spiritually intense. And so, when that's just finished, it's like a light switch goes off, and then you almost don't even know where you are.

I feel all kinds of things. I feel mostly proud. I feel really proud of myself, and I feel proud of the last dance we gave on the ballroom floor, and I feel obviously sad that it's over, that I don't get to give any more dances out there and create any more special pieces. So I think it's really both. I feel really proud of us, and I feel fulfilled, and I feel filled up, and I also feel sad that the journey of creating dances is over.

JD: When you are going through the show, it feels like any week could be you. The show is not necessarily a show about dance. It's not necessarily a competition about the best dancer. It's not about the best dance you give. It's so many other elements that go into it, which is great on a reality show front-end. It makes people tune in for all different kinds of reasons, but in doing that, you never know how it's going to go.

Once it started whittling down, it was the two of us. You kind of come to a place of like, “Okay, this could be our moment.” And I had a feeling—it was a tough week as far as some of the online noise, I would say, that goes with doing the show. So it definitely wasn't out of my mind that it could be a possibility.

Even before Jenna stepped onto the DWTS dance floor, viewers debated whether she belonged in the competition. How much prior dance experience a celebrity contestant can have—while still being considered a fair competitor—has long been a point of debate among viewers.

Jenna started her career as a dancer, where she toured alongside legendary performers, including Janet Jackson (she appeared in two music videos of the singer’s). In 2006, she landed her breakout role in Step Up, in which she played a classically trained ballerina. She was the host for television shows World of Dance and Flirty Dancing as well as a judge on Come Dance with Me. Many fans of DWTS cited Jenna’s impressive resume as an unfair advantage. “How is Jenna Dewan part of this? She was a professional dancer. Hello! So unfair already,” one X user wrote on the platform after the official season 35 cast announcement.

It should be noted, however, Jenna is not the first celebrity to join the show with previous dance experience—and it’s safe to say she’ll be far from the last. Stars like Heather Morris, Jordan Fisher, and Charli D’Amelio have all undergone criticism for joining the show in the past, despite having a substantial leg up among fellow contestants. Even Alfonso, the show’s current host and season 19 winner, had prior dance experience.

JD: I will say, through the history of watching the show and what I know about the show, is I've seen there be an issue with people with dance backgrounds, and that obviously there's a lot of opinions on whether we should even have people compete on the show that have dance backgrounds.

I definitely asked quite a few times, “Are you sure you guys want me on the show?” But the incredible people who do the show were really confident in expressing to me that this show had changed a lot, and that it’s not Dancing with the Stars Who Have Never Danced. They wanted a very dynamic cast with all different levels and strengths they bring to the ballroom. I knew it would be an uphill battle for me for sure, just from the patterns of the show and the loyalists of the show and how they feel. But ultimately, the gift of doing something just for myself was really intoxicating, and it won over any sort of doubts or hesitations I had.

JD: The hardest part of the show, I would say, is it really teaches you that joy and difficulty can exist together. There were so many highs of this journey, and then so many moments of frustration and negative noise and criticism that is honestly sad, because it tries to suck out the joy from the experience.

Even for myself with a dance background, it is vulnerable to put yourself out there in the ballroom every Tuesday and be like, “Hey guys, watch my dance and tell me what you think.” And then you have the whole other element of this social, online, noisy world that is almost like they're looking to tear people down, and I felt that that was an unfortunate shade to this show that didn't need to happen.

JD: Part of the journey of the show is interesting because for the first good couple weeks, you rarely see any of the other contestants, because you are really in your own rehearsal space, and you're just trying to get the dances down as fast as you can with your partner. I think it was rare seeing people in the hallways and connecting with some of the contestants. But yeah, we definitely would talk.

I think at one point Connor [Wood] made me laugh so hard because he said he had seen some of the online social negativity, and he said, “Everyone needs to go back to journaling.” I laughed so hard, because he is exactly right. At some point, we all thought it was okay to just get online and to be mean for no reason. We are real human beings that see this and feel this, and I think that that gets forgotten.

When we did the team dance, that was when we really were able to start bonding as the contestants, because we were finally together working towards one dance and in a room together. I absolutely love them, and we were all definitely talking about this and sharing our experiences with this, and how most of us at that point, I think, had taken it off our phone or turned off social media.

JD: Naturally, because of my dance background, there were really high expectations that I put on myself, and that the world was putting on me. I didn't even realize it was happening, but it was creating this feeling that I needed to let go of perfection and kind of just get comfortable being seen and just being there. I didn't need to prove anything.

I think I just realized how much of my life I spent wanting to get things right. And this experience really challenged me in that way, because what I realized is, you just can't grow if you're constantly worried about being perfect. I had to learn to be a little uncomfortable, to be critiqued again, to make some mistakes, to be vulnerable, and just let people see me in the middle of figuring something out. There's actually a lot of freedom in that, because I didn't have ballroom dance down perfectly by the time I got out there.

JD: I thought that every dance we did. I thought that during the week two jive, and it was intriguing to me that [the judges] were so critical of certain dances. However, when I look back, there was a lot of growth for me.

There was a whole element of this that was sort of discovering my strength in a new way because I have had three children, I've navigated huge life transitions, I've built a career, a family, a life, And now, I'm stepping into this show where I'm pushing myself physically, emotionally, creatively in a way that I haven't in years. So I think I just surprised myself with how strong I am, and not just physically, but emotionally.

Jenna also faced an unexpected complication when her partner, Val, was suspended for one episode of the show following a social media post he made about DWTS judge Carrie Ann Inaba. After Carrie Ann criticized his wife, fellow pro dancer Jenna Johnson, for including what she considered an illegal lift in her routine with Harry Shum Jr., Val posted, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night.” The now-deleted post was widely interpreted as a reference to the 2022 Academy Awards, when Will Smith slapped Chris Rock after making a joke about his wife, Jada Pinkett Smith.

Carrie Ann appeared to interpret the post as a threat. She shared a screenshot of a Page Six story about it on Instagram, writing, “So this is what we are doing now?”

On Oct. 17, DWTS production company BBC Studios said Val would not participate in the Oct. 20 episode. Jenna danced with pro Alan Bersten in his place.

JD: I said this, and I really mean this, that I did not foresee having as many challenges as I did that were thrown at me during my Dancing with the Stars journey. However, the challenges of it gave me an opportunity to walk my talk, and I always think that when that happens, you can go back to your true north, to what’s your intention for doing something. How do you want to show up as a human when you’re experiencing challenges? And I kept going back to my kids. When the mid-season suspension happened, and all these things were going on, I thought, “I have a real opportunity here. I can be annoyed and bitter and upset about this, or I can show up with grace and love and joy and focus on the moment.”

That particular week was about my mom and my dedication to her. And she was in town, thrilled to have this dance with me, and thrilled to experience this moment. And I thought that this is something she's going to remember. We're all going to remember my family forever. Let's focus on that, and let's not worry about all of this that's going on.

JD: I’ve seen that, and I feel like with just life in general, even outside of Dancing with the Stars, that is absolutely something that most females have experienced. I think there's been a great change in our world, but I think for years upon years upon years, women have had a fight against misogyny and inherent bias. Women at times in life are just held to a different standard than men, and I think that that is a real reflection.

We're expected to be exceptional, but also humble and confident, but not too confident, skilled, but not struggling enough to earn praise. There's all this pressure on women. It feels like sometimes if a woman is strong or capable, the expectations become that much higher. I think people are so busy expecting women to be extraordinary that we forget to celebrate them for being extraordinary.

JD: It's never too late for a new chapter in life. And I think if there was like, one thing I wanted people to take away from my whole journey, it’s that we're never finished becoming who we are, and it's never too late to choose your own passion in life and your own joy in life. There isn't some age where you stop growing and dreaming and trying new things.

Alyssa Cruz is the social media editor at Women’s Health, where she drives social strategy and helps shape the brand’s voice across platforms. Prior to WH, she worked at CBS News and palabra. Originally from Toledo, she is a proud alumna of Ohio University, where she received two bachelor’s degrees in journalism and Spanish. When she is not creating social content, you can find her trying different restaurants in New York City or planning her next trip.

#4927. Women Share the Best, Most Unexpected Products That Got Them Through Marathon Training

Because sometimes you don’t know you need something until it’s too late.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

There are some things you know you need before you start training for a marathon, like a good pair of sneakers. But some of the most useful marathon items? You don’t even realize how helpful they are until you’re deep in the thick of training.

We’re talking the non-glitzy, random products that make life easier when you’re spending multiple days running each week. For me, one of those things is canned salmon. I buy the stuff in bulk because when I get back from a long run, it only takes me 20 seconds to whip the stuff up with some salt, pepper, and mayo and serve it on crackers before I collapse on the couch for a few hours. (It’s a kinda-smelly, but ridiculously simple way to get protein fast.)

Curious what other unexpected finds made a difference, I asked women to share the products they never knew they needed before running a marathon but now can't imagine training without. Check out their answers…

There is nothing like race day, especially for your first marathon. And, for the most part, you know what you need: Your trusty sneakers, an outfit you’ve hopefully tested during training, your fuel, and your watch. Here are three more things that will help the day go by even better.

“Having your name on a shirt or bib is soooo fun because even strangers will cheer you on along the course! It will help you feel the true energy and vibe of the race.” —Claudette Sariya, 33, Honolulu ’25 (You can use iron-on letters from Amazon, or go through a company like Pens and Paces to commission your own bib.)

“Rally is a great way to feel supported by your loved ones who can’t make the race, or maybe you don’t have time to stop if you’re going for a personal best. At mile 10 of my first marathon, I was struggling a bit and my mom’s message came through my headphones—I hear her words every time I run a race now. Such a special concept that really enhanced my race day!” — Shannon Kauber, 25, NYC ’25, ’26, Chicago ’26

“After a race, because I have so many apps running (like Strava, Spotify, and Rally), my battery can be very low, and it sucks when I’m on four percent and looking for friends and family or want to take pictures, so it’s good to have a portable charger just in case. I’m less anxious knowing that I’ll be able to get in touch with people and that my phone is good to go. And if my phone dies randomly, then I’ll have backup juice.” —Sariya (Any charger will work, but Sariya has seen success with Anker brand ones.)

“I had my boyfriend meet me at the halfway point with a cold towel and it was a game changer. It made me feel instantly more awake and energetic.” —Tianna Soto, 32, NYC ’24, NYC Virtual ’26 (You can stay low-tech and put an old towel in the freezer, or you can opt for a cooling towel that helps you regulate your body temp.)

These products all help remove any uncomfortable rubbing and chafing from their gear to keep you comfortable over many, many miles.

“I keep it on my bathroom counter so I don’t forget to swipe at minimum inner thighs and inner arms for a training run. Long runs and race days get the full treatment with swipes under any and every seam, around the toes, waistbands, and shoulders under straps. I love traveling with the teeny travel version too.” —Jennifer Nied, 40, NYC ’17, ’19, Chicago ’18, London ’24

“The bigger ones saved me when I used to get these crazy arch blisters from when I first started running. I usually use those, but I’ve also used the smaller ones for toe blisters.” —Geneve Lau, 27, Marine Corps ’24, NYC ’25, ’26

“I swear by [these] soft little tubes that go over your toe to help prevent friction and pressure when you’re running or walking. I just started using them this year, and they’ve saved my pinkie toes during training and the marathon!” —Soto

Fueling is one of the most important parts of marathon training, and chances are you've already experimented with your fair share of gels. But sometimes, the foods and snacks you never thought to try end up making the biggest difference.

“I liked clementines as a whole food before moving to gels and chews. Clementine wedges are bite-sized so I wasn’t as worried about choking while running but they weren’t chewy, saving those textures for other fuel. They have water and sugar, though I never did the math on the amount of sugar compared to my needs while training (I know better now). During training, I would toss two whole clementines in my running hydration vest pockets and peel as I ran to occupy my hands/brain with something other than running. On race day, I pre-peeled the food and put the slices in a snack sized ziploc.” —Suzi Berkey Hanson, Chicago ’23

“As someone with endometriosis and a resulting sensitive G.I. system, taking in a high volume of carbs at any point in time is highly aggravating to my stomach and often causes high levels of nausea, bloating, and discomfort. So, I decided to switch to more solid foods that included a healthy source of fats and proteins mixed in with carbs. In this marathon training block, I would alternate Kind Bars with Honey Stinger Chews which sat much better with my stomach and made my race and post race recovery much more pleasant.” —Winnie Yu, 31, NYC ’23, ’26

“I ate one pretty much after every morning run because they were easy to throw in my bag and defrost on the way to work and they’re great for quick carbs. They were also great to eat before a long run because, again, they require basically no prep. When you’re marathon training and working a full-time job sometimes you just gravitate towards whatever is easiest and whatever fits into your routine best but still helps you meet your goals and this was mine” —Andrea Bian, 26, NYC ’25, ’26

Olivia Luppino is an associate editor at Women’s Health. She reports, writes, and edits content ranging from service stories to in-depth features and awards packages across all verticals, including health, fitness, sports, and beauty. While at WH, she’s traveled to Paris, France to watch Faith Kipyegon attempt a sub-4-minute mile and covered major races like Ultra Trail du Mont Blanc in Chamonix. Olivia is a RRCA-certified running coach who is especially passionate about helping people start their running journey and is training for her second marathon. Her works also appears in New York Magazine’s The Cut, PS (formerly Popsugar), and Salon, where she also did on-camera interviews with celebrity guests.

#4925. 17 Best Airbnb Cabins for a Picture-Perfect Outdoor Retreat (2026)

Picture this: A wood-burning stove, a claw-foot tub, no cell service, and no news. Are you in heaven? Or are you in one of the best Airbnb cabins we’ve rounded up across the US? Whether it’s an organic design marvel in Washington that would make Frank Lloyd Wright weep or a sauna-equipped “bird house” cabin in Wisconsin that piques your interest, there are so many places to enjoy the great outdoors in style. So, if immaculate cabin rentals make up your fall and winter travel mood board, look to these cozy cabins, tiny homes, chalets, and comfortable cottages for a weekend getaway. Think: elevated A-frames and Lincoln log-style beauties, fleshed out with curated amenities and thoughtful design details. Here, you can get a little lost in the beauty of the wilderness (without giving up too much in the way of modern accommodations).

Perks: Indoor fireplace, private patio, barbecue grill, sound system, security system, free parking

A steeply pitched roof and black metal siding give this tiny cabin near Oregon’s Mount Hood a striking silhouette against the towering pines. Designed by a professional architect, the 190-square-foot retreat takes its cues from shinrin-yoku, the Japanese practice of forest bathing. The exterior pairs dark metal with warm pine cladding, while oversized windows look out to picturesque woodland views. Inside, there's a sound system, queen bed, wood-burning stove, and compact kitchenette, but the real luxury is falling asleep to natural white noise from the surrounding forest. Even the shower comes with a forest view, making this a particularly appealing place to spend a weekend off the grid. From $381 per night.

Perks: Mountain views, forest views, private balcony, fireplace, fire pit, nearby hiking trails, nearby skiing, private security

At nearly 11,000 feet above sea level, this Breckenridge cabin puts you practically eye to eye with Colorado’s towering Quandary Peak. Getting there involves climbing about 60 steps through the evergreens, but the payoff is a private balcony with sweeping mountain views. Inside, the renovated retreat has a Scandinavian-inspired aesthetic, with warm wood finishes, cozy textiles, and a gas fireplace for snowy evenings. A spiral staircase leads to the sleeping quarters, while outside, a firepit offers another spot to take in the alpine scenery. Downtown Breckenridge is just 15 minutes away, though between the mountain views and the deck, there’s plenty of incentive to stay put. From $365 per night.

Perks: Mountain view, wood-fired hot tub, indoor fireplace, fire pit, private backyard, hiking, free parking

The Blue Ridge Mountains are the main attraction at Doah House, a cabin perched high above Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley. A 16-foot wall of sliding glass doors opens onto a wraparound deck, making the one-of-a-kind forest views visible from anywhere in the living room. Inside the blonde wood interiors, a wood-burning stove, heated floors, and a lofted bedroom equipped with a queen-sized bed add to the appeal. The bathroom features Moroccan tile, a rainfall shower, and a floor-to-ceiling window overlooking the trees. Outside, a private wood-fired hot tub and firepit make a strong case for spending the evening at the cabin, though Shenandoah National Park, Appalachian Trail hikes, and local wineries are all within reach. From $204 per night.

Perks: Mountain views, hot tub, sauna, fire pit, wood-burning stove, BBQ grill, heated bathroom floors free parking

Fresh eggs from the chicken coop, herbs picked straight from the garden, and a creekside sauna are just a few of the unexpected perks at Firelight at Shope Creek, a collection of eight cabins spread across 22 wooded acres outside Asheville, North Carolina. Cozy flourishes fill this 650-square-foot retreat with modern design, like a wood-burning stove, heated bathroom floors, and a spacious deck overlooking the surrounding mountains and meadows. There's also a private hot tub just steps from the king-size bedroom, ideally positioned for stargazing after dark. Guests can wander the property's private hiking trails, gather around the communal firepits, or settle into the covered outdoor pavilion, which has its own fireplace. And despite the secluded setting, downtown Asheville and the Blue Ridge Parkway are only about 20 minutes away. From $320 per night.

Perks: Hiking trails, swimming, hot tub, fire pit, sound system, fireplace, washer/dryer

During the day, a generous amount of sunlight pours into this secluded Maine cabin, illuminating thoughtful architectural details like floor-to-celing wood paneled walls and heightened ceilings. After sunset, a well-curated lighting scheme sets the mood, affording the opportunity to test-drive the property’s record player sound system and transform the main living area into a vinyl listening den. Don’t expect to spend all your time indoors, though. Outside of this modern cabin, there’s no shortage of adventures to explore, from swimming in the lake to hiking one of several nature trails close by. Boating rentals and the local golf course offer even more ways to spend your stay, as well as winter skiing or snowboarding just a 40-minute drive away. From $645 per night.

Perks: Ocean view, shared outdoor pool, sauna, fireplace, beach access

Private and serene, sweeping views of the Pacific Ocean surround this Sea Ranch cabin escape that meets the California coast. Best suited for a couples getaway or a duo vacation, an open floor plan and 30-foot-high ceilings ensure that the space doesn’t feel overly cramped, while oversized windows drench the rental in sunlight on cloudless days. Modern upgrades like minimalist furniture silhouettes, recognizable decor, and an updated kitchen bring contemporary flair to the home’s original timber frame built back in 1965. Outside, an expansive deck overlooking the nearby meadow is a natural place to enjoy morning coffee or your current novel. Walk along the bluff to one of several bordering beaches, or visit one of the private recreation centers to work on your tennis backhand or swimming skills indoors. From $681 per night.

Perks: Lake view, fireplace, BBQ grill, fire pit, free parking, washer/dryer

Tucked among the Wisconsin woodlands, MetalLark Tower is surrounded by impressive views, supplied by the nearby wildflower meadow and clandestine lake. The 800-square-foot home’s interiors are equally noteworthy, following modern Scandinavian design principles that make the space feel intentional and cozy. (Think: simple furniture silhouettes and a neutral color palette with light wood tones contrasted by stark black and grey accents). When you’re not admiring the dramatic floor-to-ceiling windows with stunning, 360-degree views of the region, the outdoor living area has lots to offer, like a lounge area, fire pit, and grill. From $379 per night.

Perks: Outdoor showers, hot tub, fire pit

Checking into this tree-flanked cabin in Wartburg feels like stepping into a luxurious nature retreat. Maybe it’s the pair of waffle robes hung outside the private hot tub deck, or the modern Adirondacks arranged around the fire pit facing the tree line. But that’s just the beginning of the relaxation you’ll experience in your secluded private rental. Here, sliding doors and windows invite you to commune with the great outdoors from every room, while the clean, Scandinavian-style interiors align with the space’s overwhelmingly calming atmosphere. The Solenne is a picture-perfect vacation spot for two, with a king-size floating bed that ensures no one is fighting for space. Consider staying here for a honeymoon, a romantic winter getaway, or a restful solo trip down south. From $219 per night.

#4924. Here’s what happened in crypto today

Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.

Today in crypto, former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson called on Britain to lead in blockchain development despite his persistent skepticism of Bitcoin, Harvard and Dartmouth maintained their holdings in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF during the third quarter, and Bitcoin mining services provider Luxor warned of increasingly frequent AI-enabled cyberattacks after its platform was compromised.

Former United Kingdom Prime Minister Boris Johnson has backed blockchain technology and tokenization as opportunities for the UK’s financial sector, despite persistent doubts about cryptocurrencies.

Speaking at Solana’s Breakpoint conference in London on Monday, Johnson maintained his position that Bitcoin (BTC) resembles a Ponzi scheme, following an opinion piece published in the Daily Mail in March. He questioned who investors could hold accountable if funds were stolen.

However, Johnson distinguished his criticism of digital assets from his view of the underlying technology, saying the UK should be at the forefront of tokenization.

Lord Ross Kempsell, who joined Johnson on stage, said although he shared his reservations on cryptocurrencies, “on the parts of the industry that can be brought into a regulated perimeter, which the regulators are working on, there’s a lot of scope here for a high growth industry.”

Harvard University and Dartmouth College reported unchanged share counts in BlackRock’s spot Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF) at the end of the third quarter as a Bitcoin rally lifted the value of both stakes.

Harvard held 3.04 million shares of the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT), worth about $144.1 million at the end of September, while Dartmouth reported 201,531 shares valued at $9.5 million, according to Form 13F filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

IBIT gained about 42% in Q3 as Bitcoin rallied nearly 43%. Both posted their strongest quarterly gains of 2026 through September.

Harvard has reported the same IBIT share count since the end of March, after cutting its holdings by 43% in Q1 and 21% in Q4 2025. Dartmouth has reported the same 201,531 shares since first disclosing its Bitcoin ETF position in Q4 2025.

Bitcoin mining services provider Luxor has warned that AI-enabled cyberattacks are becoming increasingly difficult to defend against after attackers compromised its mining-management platform and redirected customers’ computing power to another mining pool over the weekend.

In an X post on Sunday, Luxor CEO Nick Hansen said the attack came through a “sophisticated AI-enabled vector,” without specifying how AI was used in the attack, warning that these types of attacks will only get more frequent over time.

“At this moment, anyone running any sort of substantial business, especially in crypto, is inundated with AI-enabled attacks,” Hansen said in an X post. “This does not seem to be slowing down; rather, it’s speeding up as models get better and more attackers enter the arena.”

The warning comes as security researchers have documented the spread of AI-assisted hacking tools, raising the prospect of faster attacks against businesses holding money or controlling valuable infrastructure.

#4921. 9 Best Duvet Covers: Editor Sets to Style a Bedscape (2026)

Besides pieces like quilts and coverlets, I always say duvet covers are the best accessories to give a bedscape a bit more personality. Take it from Ariel Kaye, founder of juggernaut bedding brand Parachute, who has filled her eclectic LA home with a range of duvet covers that span vibrant, breezy linens to neutral, crisp percales.

To truly find the best of the best, I rounded up a group of writers and editors to test duvet covers from our favorite bedding brands—featuring muted, structured covers for minimalists and trendy colorways and patterns for maximalists. As for our top pick, we went with Boll & Branch’s Signature Hemmed Duvet Set since it’s organic, has a smooth and breathable feel, and comes in tons of prints and colors for easy styling.

If you’re still on the fence about what to go with for your bedroom, I also tapped AD PRO Directory designers to share what they look for in duvet covers, including materiality and design. Read below to create your dream bedscape this season.

For consistency, all prices listed reflect queen-size duvets unless otherwise noted, but up to king sizes are available for purchase from each brand.

Boll & Branch is one of AD’s favorite brands when it comes to bedding. With super soft sheets and other products made from 100% organic cotton, they have a heavy focus on sustainability and directly sourcing raw materials. The duvet cover follows suit, with long-staple cotton making for a durable piece of bedding that I’ve found is breathable enough for both hot and cold nights.

This organic-cotton duvet set can please pretty much anyone with a traditional bedroom. It has a tried-and-true cotton sateen material that gets softer with every wash, and designs—including subtle botanical prints—that are a must for anyone with classic taste. The earthy tones are great for a grounded bedroom too.

Bring the outdoors in with your styling by pairing one of Boll & Branch’s botanical prints with a textured linen sheet set.

Shop AD editors have stood behind Boll & Branch for years because of the brand’s sustainable business model and high-quality bedding. The signature cotton sheets have even earned a top spot in our best-of guides for the last five years. Just like these sheets, shopping producer Lauren Arzbaecher tells me that this Boll & Branch duvet cover’s sateen weave has a buttery soft texture. “The cotton is very smooth, and I maintained a comfortable temperature throughout the night even when bundled up underneath all my bedding,” she says. As a cold sleeper, Arzbeacher loves layering extra throws and blankets on top of her duvet, and she says this ultra-breathable material has all the “cuddly qualities” you’d want without making you overheat. Even better, the bedding is 100% organic, so you can rest knowing you’re not breathing in any harmful chemicals.

This sateen duvet cover also has a zipper closure, so it’s a lot easier for Arzbaecher to slip her Company Store down insert on and off than other button-closure covers she’s tried. “Their solid color range has a lovely mix of earthy hues, and the brand has been releasing more and more patterns, from stripes to florals,” for styling a bed, she adds.

I’m not sure what’s left to say about this bedding brand that hasn’t already been plastered across subway ads or Instagram feeds, but in short, Brooklinen is somewhat of a bedding celebrity. It has garnered cool-kid status by offering top-quality products using Oeko-Tex-certified products at reasonable prices.

The Classic Duvet Cover is made of percale, which can be compared to a crisp cotton button-down shirt. It’s soft and sophisticated in a matte, buttery finish that can be attributed to long-staple cotton fibers that are spun to make stronger but finer yarn.

We are not only big fans of Brooklinen products for their breathable, sustainable materials but also for their versatile designs. With 20 earthy tones, I recommend this duvet cover for any type of bedroom style—but I’d lean towards purchasing for a coastal design because of the soothing colors and prints.

Like Alpert, who has this duvet cover in her bedroom, I recommend styling it with textured linen sheets for a contrasting yet comfortable fabric combination and a throw blanket in complementary neutral and oceanic hues.

Not one but two AD writers love this Brooklinen cotton duvet cover all year long. Shopping writer Julia Harrison calls this super, super soft and very cool to the touch. “It stays cool even when I’ve wrapped myself all the way in it like a caterpillar so I’m never overheating, but I am staying comfy and warm,” she shares. Contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert says this is her favorite duvet cover of all time, hands-down, because of its unmatched airy and parachute-like quality. “The percale duvet cover has this smooth feel but at the same time it is remarkably light and crisp,” she says. “Apparently, it’s all because of the high-quality single-ply yarns, which are made from strong, long-staple cotton fibers that give it that buttery touch.”

The style potential is a plus here too. Alpert loves the “oyster” print since it strays away from more expected patterns like stripes filling up her linen closet. She got the matching sheets in the same print for this exact reason, saying the swirls remind her of “Hokusai’s waves and stand out in the sea of florals and plaids” in her linen closet.

From pajamas to sheets, Cozy Earth is a favorite of ours—and Oprah thanks to frequent appearances in her Favorite Things lists—for cooling bedding made of bamboo fabric. Its offerings also ring in at a budget-friendly price (especially with the brand’s frequent sales).

Many of the colors in Cozy Earth’s collection are grounded in the earth (to be expected). With this in mind, I see this duvet cover in a minimalist, bohemian, or coastal bedroom. Alpert’s peony pick is just as nice for a romantic bedroom or something seasonal for summer.

The delicate nature of the bedding (both in texture and color) makes it a striking contrast against crisp, patterned accents, like a percale floral sheet set.

When I asked Alpert what her favorite qualities are about Cozy Earth’s signature, silky duvet cover, there were almost too many to count. “This duvet cover is a trifecta of perks: It looks good, feels good, and won’t slip off the comforter,” she says. “But if I had to pick one, I’d say that I love the delicate pink hue and the equally delicate feel of the cover—just looking at my bed makes me want to crawl into it.”

The material (100% viscose from bamboo) has a breathable and smooth feel to it that’s nice for hot sleepers but also anyone who doesn’t want a more textured cover like linen. Even better, the soft, pastel-inspired color options like peony pink and laurel green make it a great fit for styling a bed during this blooming season. “The fabric is so delicate and dreamy that it reminds me of flower petals,” Alpert tells me. “Since I chose the peony colorway, it definitely fits the romantic profile.”

Even though it has a smooth texture, the comforter inside won’t slip around because of the secure snap closures. “Cozy Earth has 12(!) points of contact between the comforter and the cover, so there is no way anything is going to get loose, especially because these are snapped on, and not tied, like many other duvet covers,” she says. “I pair it with the bamboo viscose comforter with standard fill and the combination works great because the comforter has some weight and the duvet cover does not mess with it in any way.”

A darling of the 2010s direct to consumer movement, Parachute is a home brand best known for its bedding, though the company has also dabbled in furniture, mattresses, and other essentials. Its products, including the Linen Duvet Cover, are Oeko-Tex Standard 100–certified, meaning that every element (even buttons!) has been tested for substances damaging to human health. Parachute also doesn’t artificially soften their products. In the wrong hands, linen can be itchy or stiff until it’s been broken in, but that wasn’t the case here. This version, made of European Flax and made in the Guimarães region of Portugal, was inviting and oh so soft. The company also touts the material as naturally antimicrobial, which is a plus.

Another pick for a bohemian bedroom, this duvet cover has a lived-in look and several organic colors to choose from.

If you, in true minimalist fashion, like a monochrome bedscape, style this duvet cover with linen sheets in natural colors. If you want a slightly moodier bedroom, try a shade like cacao or indigo.

Contributor Lila Allen has nothing but good things to say about the feel of this linen and its nonchalant elegance: “I was pleasantly surprised at how soft this cover was—with linen, sometimes it can be a roll of the dice. This set had the best of both worlds: super supple but still casually elevated. The linen is a nice thickness, too; I can’t see any trace of the duvet inside of it.” Parachute’s linen has 175 GSM, and Quince’s linen that I mention down below has around 150 GSM. To Allen’s point, this means Parachute’s is more durable with a substantial feel and less opaque (the reason why she can’t see her duvet insert peeking through) with a lighter cover color like toast or sand.

Allen pairs her duvet cover with an all-season comforter from Riley, which she says stays secure through a button closure on the side and gives just the right amount of rumple together. The insert moves around a bit inside of the cover but mostly remains in place. “Best of all, I’ve been sleeping soundly with the set on hot nights as well as ones where the AC has been on overdrive, and so far it holds up in both situations—not too warm or cool.” Allen tells me that she shares a bed with her “hot-blooded husband and a large Maine Coon cat,” so her bed usually runs warm. This layerable, snuggly cover is perfect.

The home brand is headquartered in New York City, however, the materials are sourced from fourth-generation, family-owned textile mills in Portugal and other countries across Europe. The products span a range of bedding and bath products, namely duvet covers, sheets, towels, mats, and other accessories like pillows and robs.

Since all of the duvet covers come in neutral, unfussy colors, this is a great option for minimalists.

I style this simply with other neutrals like white or cream sheets. When I want to add more visual interest, I layer in butter yellow bedding or a quilt in soft, muted tones.

To put it simply, this duvet cover feels like a lightweight cashmere sweater. It’s not stuffy, but it’s not flimsy either. Riley Home’s somehow managed to make a cover that feels airy enough for nights when my apartment’s radiator runs overly hot and still warm enough when I want to curl up in bed after a cold commute from work.

Even though it feels soft, it’s not made of pure cashmere. In reality, it’s made of 95% cotton and just 5% cashmere, but I wouldn’t have noticed if I didn’t read the label so closely. The texture has a brushed quality to it that feels gentle and light on my skin. There are a few neutral colors on the site. I went with the oatmeal and have liked styling it with white sheet sets so far for a simple, not-overly-done-up bedspread. A couple of other thoughtful details are the interior ties and buttons to keep my comforter from shifting inside. The super-easy care sold me too. The brand doesn’t recommend dry cleaning—just a machine wash and dry with a gentle detergent will do. As someone who has lugged specialty cashmere bedding to NYC cleaners on foot through the years, this note in and of itself almost convinced me to give the bedding a try.

Quince’s entire deal is about making high-quality luxury products at an affordable price. They work only with factories that are both sustainable and pay a fair wage, which is something that many shoppers care enough about to pay a little extra for, but Quince cuts back on things like fancy packaging to keep costs down.

Quince is another AD favorite for its plethora of prints and solid colors. Try this duvet cover in your space—no matter its design style—for a lightweight addition to your bedscape that’s also budget friendly.

Since linen makes a statement on its own with its lived-in look, I recommend styling this duvet cover with Quince’s classic European linen sheet set and a fluffy duvet insert in moody neutral hues (think deep brown) for a cozy sleep oasis. It’s also neutral enough that you can add some pattern sheeting for extra personality.

I’ve had this Quince linen duvet for about a year and it’s been a mainstay since it’s substantial and textured while still having an airiness to it—even when I’m layering with a few throw blankets or quilts when it’s cold outside. Sometimes linen gets a bad rap for its rough texture, but this best seller has been gentle against my skin and only gotten softer with more routine wear and care. It’s not as soft as something like an heirloom-quality stonewashed linen, but I’m not too picky in the linen department. I think its Oeko-Tex certification gives it a leg up generally to some competitors in this fabric category too.

I chose this Quince duvet since there were so many color options to choose from. I love moody colors year-round, and the burgundy is true to the deep color I saw on the site and it hasn’t faded after months of washes. It has the relaxed look you know and love with linen materials. Steaming it knocks out wrinkles easily whenever I want a more put-together look in my bedroom, though.

At this price point and with the most colors and prints available in this guide, I think this comforter cover can give you a great, budget-friendly way to dress a bed. The button closures also help keep a duvet insert or comforter in place. The care has been simple. I wash it with similar colors on a cold cycle and tumble dry on low and have only noticed a loose thread here and there, but nothing too crazy.

As mentioned above in our top overall pick, Brooklinen is known as the “home of the internet’s favorite sheets,” so we find it to be a worthy destination for quality bedding—including this quilt-like duvet cover made with 100% cotton.

With a design that mirrors the appearance of a quilt, we think this duvet cover would dress a vintage-inspired space beautifully—like the bedding you’d find in a historic Victorian home.

Alpert chose the plum colorway because of its sophisticated look that anchors her bedroom. She shares that the hue looks exceptionally well-paired with the deep caramel of the Boll & Branch Grand waffle blanket, as the color almost works like a moody neutral.

Even though the Brooklinen website describes this duvet as “breezy,” Alpert says it feels more like a weighted blanket. “The ribbed side is certainly quilt-like, which is not surprising because each ribbon that runs through the duvet cover is padded ever so slightly,” she shares.

The cover has a two-sided design: one side with textured, ribbed matelasse and the other with a crisp percale fabric. Alpert thinks this material combo is genius since it keeps the duvet cover from feeling too heavy. “This is especially key for anyone who sleeps without a flat sheet—you’ll feel like you’re getting into freshly changed linens night after night,” she says. “On the flip side, the ribbed texture elevates the duvet cover, not only in how it looks but it gives your bedding a slightly cushy sensation.”

Rest assured that the feel isn’t as heavy as an actual weighted blanket. Alpert says it certainly has substance and structure, though. “When I sleep with it on, it feels as if I am very secure—no one will dare wake me up,” she notes.

Hommey is a relatively new Australian-based brand that got its start in 2020. It became popular for robes and nightwear in bold, fashionable stripes. The designs are now spread across the bedding category, including cotton and linen sheets and duvet covers.

Since the brand is known for more out-of-the-box colorways across its collections, this duvet color is a great option for maximalists looking to experiment with bold color-blocking.

For a moodier bedscape, I style this duvet cover with sheets in a deep tone like burgundy. Overall, the chocolatey hue acts like a neutral and pairs beautifully with lighter sheet colors like oatmeal, which can also complement the cream-colored trim.

I know we’ve talked about linen a couple of times already in this story, but Hommey’s duvet helps hit the trifecta for the category. The natural flax fiber felt smoother and more broken-in than my Quince version right out the package. My guess is that it’s because of the stonewashed finish, which is known to give scratchy linen a more silky quality. I won’t get ahead of myself and say it feels like pure silk, but I can confirm that it’s soft and breathable almost like an organic cotton duvet after a few washes. The duvet caught my attention even more because of all of the styles. There are over 30 fashionable colors and prints, like the oxford and plum reversible cotton duvet I want in a button-down shirt version. The linen offering has four distinct colorways, including the brown sugar with cream trim that I got for myself. I like deep colors for my bedscape, especially as the year starts inching towards fall and winter, and its rich hue hasn’t disappointed. It's the perfect complement to my autumnal color palette, especially when I pair it with burgundy linen sheets.

It is less expensive than the Parachute pick and has a plusher texture than the Quince, so I’d say this is the perfect middle ground for an approachable but high-quality linen duvet.

Garnet Hill was founded in New Hampshire in the mid-1970s by Pegge and Grant Dowse who built the brand on a commitment to sustainable materials, thoughtful craftsmanship, and responsible sourcing with products like organic cotton and flannel bedding. The bedding blends traditional styles with a modern touch to fit in a range of bedrooms.

Our tester says the Pear Garden print is completely unexpected. “As much as I love florals, stripes, and gingham, a girl needs a break…and these charming pears are just the right motif,” Alpert shares. “They signal a cottagecore moment without going over the top. Every time I glimpse the cheery yellow fruit, I crack a little smile. Plus, the colorway of bold yellow, sage green, brown, and cream are easy to coordinate with the rest of my bedding collection.”

Because the pear motifs are the statement, we think you can go with more subtle sheets like a white set with embroidered trim. If you’re more of a maximalist, you can lean into the pattern play with a gingham sheet set in a complementary muted tone like brown and extra layers like a faux fur blanket if you’re cozying up for winter.

According to Alpert, this duvet cover is synonymous with cozy. It’s the softest option on this list because of the brushed flannel fabric, and it’s also a great pick if you live in cold climates since it has a bit of heft to it. “It’s as if a layer of leaves, or in this case pears, is surrounding me during winter hibernation,” she says. “That’s in part because this specific flannel is woven to have a substantial six-ounce weight.”

Alpert’s had this for nearly one year and says it has a decadent texture, likening it to climbing under a layer of meringue when she pairs it with her fluffy Ostermoor down duvet insert. “The plush feel of the cover also makes me think that I’ve just scored an upgrade to a royal suite,” Alpert adds.

At this point, she hasn’t noticed any pilling, but she does note that the cover is a bit snugger than a typical king, so you can expect the duvet to feel a little loftier than a regular fit.

What to Look for in the Best Duvet Covers

A duvet cover is more than just a bedcover. This eye-catching textile has a large footprint in any bedroom and can instantly give your space a refresh—whether with unique colors and prints or something more modest—especially if you want to disguise an old duvet insert. With this in mind, I tapped AD PRO Directory designers to weigh in on what to look for in a duvet cover to elevate your bedroom.

Material: When it comes to duvet covers, everyone has their own personal preferences. For Nicole R. Fisher, CEO and founder of Nicole Fisher Interiors, it’s linen: “They’re effortless, lightweight, and airy. I think the simplicity of the linen transcends different styles and spaces,” she says. Fisher notes that the feel is a big factor when selecting a duvet cover.

Carmen René Smith, founder and principal designer of Aquilo Interiors, says that it also needs to feel soft to the touch, breathable, and cozy. “What’s the point of a beautiful duvet if you don’t want to snuggle into it?” she says. “Texture is key too—whether it’s silky, crisp, or nubby, it should add depth to the space.”

Comfort: All of the interior designers I spoke to for this story point to natural fibers, not only because of their quality but also their airflow and breathability. Shelbie Cox of Shelbie Cox Studio recommends natural fibers like organic cotton and linen and notes that polyester and other synthetic fibers are best to avoid since they can trap heat.

Design: With so many patterns and colors to choose from, it’s important to keep your bedroom’s design style in mind. If you like more of a minimalist bedroom, Cox suggests a fine stripe pattern (like Quince’s European Linen Duvet Cover) or a monochromatic, muted color palette (see the Cozy Earth Bamboo Duvet Cover) for your duvet cover set.

If you want to go bold for your bedroom, there are options aplenty. “We’re maximalists, so we say bump up the color and pattern no matter what your signature style is!” says Smith, adding that it’s important to still maintain balance. “If you have bold wallpaper, pull a color from it and go for a solid, textured duvet—like a rich velvet for drama or a soft linen for a more relaxed vibe. If you’re mixing patterns, think about scale—a bold, oversized print pairs best with a smaller, more delicate duvet pattern to give the eye a place to rest.”

If you don’t want to commit to one style just yet, rest assured that having a few duvets in rotation can help you keep your bedroom design fresh. “I tend to go simple on bedding and let the accessories be the pops of pattern and color that’s easily swapped out,” adds Fisher.

Maintenance: While these are great design accessories for a bedroom, they also need to be practical. Ashley Ross, founder and principal designer of Muse Noire Interiors recommends keeping these questions in mind when shopping: How does it fasten (zipper, tie up, or buttons)? Does it fit within your washer and dryer? This will help you know how to use it and how to care for it.

We tested the best duvet covers the same way we test products for the rest of our sleep content: by bringing the items in our homes and dressing them on our beds. This way, you’re guaranteed to get a real-life look at how the products perform after weeks and months of everyday use. We also wash them routinely to keep an eye out for any wear and tear. All of the brands we feature reflect a variety of price points, designs, and materials so you have the best options to choose from for your bedroom.

Jump to the “How We Tested” section of this article to watch an in-depth video about our testing methodology and some of our favorite products and brands.

You don’t necessarily need a duvet cover. It depends on how you like to dress your bed. In my opinion, it’s a great bed accessory. A duvet cover not only protects your duvet insert but it also gives you the opportunity to easily switch up your bedscape (instead of swapping comforters when you want a new look). That said, pay attention to the care instructions for your insert because some do not recommend washing or dry cleaning.

There are several ways you can put a duvet cover on, but according to TikTok experts, this method below is as foolproof as possible:

Start by turning your duvet cover inside out, top side down, with the duvet opener at the foot of the bed. Then, place your comforter on top and secure the corners with the attached ties to the duvet cover. Starting at the head of the bed, roll the duvet down towards the foot just like a burrito. Finally, fold the duvet opening over each end of the roll, and unroll the blanket back towards the

Always check the manufacturer instructions to find out how to wash your specific duvet cover. However, the most common way to clean a duvet cover is by machine washing it with like colors with a gentle detergent on a cold cycle. If the duvet cover has a zipper closure, it's usually helpful to zip it closed to keep it from snagging in the washing machine.

It's generally recommended to wash your duvet cover as often as you wash your sheets, which is about once a week. If you use a top sheet, though, you can usually extend another week and wash your duvet cover every other week.

Our editors selected top products in this story from tried-and-true brands on the market, from Brooklinen to Boll & Branch. These brands boast organic materials like 100% organic cotton and European Flax and bamboo for a sustainably made bed. Plus, many boast eco-friendly certifications like GOTS and Oeko-Tex so you know they are free of chemicals. As a design editor, I also made sure all of the products have a range of colors, patterns, and prints to complement a bedroom’s style.

#4916. Binance hack may push institutions to outside custody, FalconX exec says

FalconX’s Joshua Lim says the Binance hack could push institutions to keep crypto off exchanges and change how large investors trade in 2027.

A major shift in institutional crypto trading could be on the horizon following the recent Binance hack, as security concerns may lead to more large investors keeping their assets outside exchanges, according to a FalconX executive.

In an exclusive interview with Cointelegraph at the Digital Asset Forum in New York City on Nov. 13, Joshua Lim, global head of markets at FalconX, a digital asset brokerage for institutional investors, said the Oct. 29 hack could make institutions more cautious about trading crypto and change how they store their assets.

“It’s actually quite bearish for more institutional participation in crypto,” Lim told Cointelegraph. He said traders initially played down the hack but later began to recognize its potential long-term impact.

As a result, Lim expects more institutions to turn to outside custody providers and trading firms that allow them to trade without keeping their crypto on exchanges, a shift he believes could become one of the biggest trends in 2027.

North Korean-linked hackers stole about $6.4 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, making it the largest crypto theft on record, according to blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis.

The shift toward keeping crypto outside exchanges already appeared to be underway even before the hack. In an October proposal, the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said industry practices were developing that reduced the need to move investment advisers’ client assets and regulated funds’ crypto holdings out of permitted custody for trading.

Lim pointed to Copper, a crypto custody provider, as one company that could benefit. Its ClearLoop service lets investors trade on supported exchanges while keeping their crypto with a separate company.

Copper said collateral protected by its ClearLoop service supported more than $240 billion in perpetual futures trading volume during the first quarter of 2026, more than double the amount a year earlier.

Lim explained that investors can keep their assets outside an exchange while receiving credited balances that allow them to trade on it. Under the brokerage model Lim described, a hedge fund can place trades through FalconX, which executes them using its own exchange accounts and relationships. Still, investors face risks tied to the firms holding their assets and settling their trades.

“For many players, facing a regulated entity like ours is more palatable,” Lim added.

Related: Crypto hack losses equal 57 cents per $1 earned onchain: Ark’s Valente

Binance recorded large Bitcoin outflows in mid-November, although it is not clear whether they were linked to the hack.

According to CryptoQuant data, Binance recorded net withdrawals of about 2,771 Bitcoin (BTC) on Friday, followed by 2,708 BTC on Saturday and 5,636 BTC on Sunday — totaling about 11,115 BTC leaving the exchange than entered over those three days.

The withdrawals came as the broader crypto market was falling, with Bitcoin trading around $65,000 at 9:41 pm UTC Monday, down about 20% over the past month, according to CoinGecko.

However, the data does not show who moved the Bitcoin or why. Investors could have transferred their funds to personal wallets, companies that store crypto on their behalf, or to other exchanges.

Beyond concerns about exchange security, Lim expects other changes in how large investors trade in 2027. He said institutions want more ways to trade assets such as oil, gold and stock market indexes through crypto platforms, including outside regular market hours.

“You can respond quickly to news events when they happen,” Lim said, citing one of the benefits of 24/7 trading.

That type of trading is already taking place on Hyperliquid, a decentralized trading platform that offers contracts tied to traditional assets. As of Monday, Hyperliquid’s markets for traditional assets and other contracts had about $4.3 billion in open interest and recorded $3.9 billion in trading volume over 24 hours, according to data from Perpys.

But while crypto platforms are giving investors more ways to trade, Lim said the financial services needed to support those trades have not kept up, particularly when it comes to borrowing money and managing risk.

For example, investors can now trade oil through traditional futures markets, investment funds and crypto platforms. But lenders may treat trades on each platform separately, even when those trades balance each other out.

“There’s not enough players that can give you leverage or margin financing against all of these things collectively,” Lim said. “The risk netting is not quite there yet.”

#4914. Artists Helen Marden and the Late Brice Marden Refashioned a Decommissioned 19th-Century Ferry Terminal

Over the course of their more than 50-year marriage, artist Helen Marden and her late husband, the eminent painter Brice Marden, amassed an international collection of seriously eccentric—and deeply magical—houses, gardens, and studios, each designed around the double helix of art and family. They bought their first house, a cliffside cottage on the Greek island of Hydra, in 1973, and since then real estate and art have been entwined in their life, art facilitating the purchase of property, the properties both catalyst and carapace for the evolution of their art. An Italianate villa in upstate New York, a pair of traditional riads in Marrakech, a hotel set among the ruins of a 19th-century sugar plantation in the Caribbean, a second house by the port in Hydra, a Renaissance Revival town house in Manhattan, a stately manse on a sprawling estate in Pennsylvania—every one of their idiosyncratic properties has its own fascinating history, reflected in its interior. The homes are all documented in the upcoming book Brice & Helen Marden: Houses, Gardens, Studios (Gagosian), edited by this writer, with photography by Stephen Kent Johnson.

Helen Marden in the living room. Chair and side table by the Campana Brothers. The chimney is clad in Clé Tile. A watercolor by Henri Michaux rests on the mantel.

The living room includes chairs by Marcel Wanders (far left) and the Campana Brothers. Sculpture at right by Michael Wang.

In the dining room, a Paavo Tynell pendant hangs above a rustic farm table with chairs by Jonathan Olivares and Maarten Baas. Amazonia marble covers one wall.

The Mardens were instinctively drawn to residences with endurance, places that have seen a few things, not newly built pleasure domes devoid of texture and soul. Swan House, the riparian hideaway in the middle of the Hudson River, epitomizes the couple’s embrace of the strange and the enchanted. Accessed by a long, narrow causeway that leads off the shore of Saugerties, the structure was built in 1877 as part of Long Dock, a ship terminal and moorage for large vessels conveying people and goods the length of the Hudson. It was also a landing for ferries crossing the river between Saugerties and the village of Tivoli. One can see Swan House shimmering in the landscape from the edge of Rose Hill, the Marden family’s 19th-century Tivoli estate.

The Depression, along with the advent of more efficient modes of transport, scuppered the last of the large ships landing at Long Dock in the early 1930s, but ferries continued to make the two-minute trip across the water until 1938. After that, the structure was decommissioned from professional service and sold, becoming the only privately owned peninsula on the Hudson. The Mardens purchased the property in 2011, but it took a full decade before they engaged designer Daniel Sachs and architect Kevin Lindores of the AD100 firm Sachs Lindores Architecture, Interiors to execute a full-scale renovation.

The primary bath features custom zellige tiles, a vintage Vistosi chandelier, an antique marble sink, and a tub by The Water Monopoly.

Sachs Lindores remodeled the entry with a windscreen of glass brick. The chair is by Gaetano Pesce.

Yellow zellige tiles meet a pale pink Aga range beneath a custom zinc hood in the kitchen. The pendant light is by Adolf Loos from WOKA.

Brice Marden’s For Helen – Valentine 2019 (2015–18) hangs on the black-tiled fireplace tower that mediates the bedroom and living room.

A custom bed is flanked by an antique French console table and a Charles Rohlfs hall chair. Lighting includes a Franz West chandelier and a floor lamp by Achille and Pier Giacomo Castiglioni.

“Early on we demolished a few walls to open up the views, but it was pretty raw. We’d just go over and watch the boats go by,” Helen recalls. “You have a completely different relationship with the river when you’re sitting in the middle of it.”

Given the famously cultivated, idiosyncratic tastes of the homeowners, the collaboration between Sachs Lindores and their clients was unusually fertile. Together, they reimagined the derelict building as a trick box for trapping the natural light that bounces off the water on all sides, with reflective, lead-coated copper siding and a zinc roof on the exterior and fields of luminous plaster, tile, and marble within. “Helen never shies away from a bold gesture. At first, she told us to paint the house red, but when we presented the idea of a glistening metal-clad box with light dancing on the skin, she immediately went for it,” Sachs recalls. “Brice and Helen were very interconnected in their aesthetic tastes and decision making,” Lindores adds. “As you might imagine, they studied every paint color and trim detail.”

Ruins of the 19th-century dock remain alongside the house.

A guest room is outfitted with a Pierre Jeanneret daybed, lounge chairs by Monika Mulder for IKEA, a vintage Kevin Walz standing lamp, and a Mathieu Matégot magazine rack. Painting by Helen Marden.

Sigmar Polke’s Untitled (1998) hangs above a vintage Walter Knoll sofa in the first-floor sitting room.

While retaining the shape of its original architectural envelope, the house was essentially rebuilt, with new window configurations, open circulation, and an exposed ceiling, all in service of maximizing watery vistas and ease of use. On the lofty upper level, the existing chimney, newly revealed in its full floor-to-ceiling height, was clad in glossy black brick tile. The monolithic form now feels like a high altar in a temple of light. Custom zellige tiles imported from Fez cover the walls of the kitchen and baths, where Helen’s genius for juxtaposing colors and materials comes into high relief.

The polyglot ensemble of furnishings hews closely to the signature Marden mix: Moroccan rugs; bold contemporary designs by the likes of Gaetano Pesce, Marcel Wanders, and the Campana Brothers; humble American folk pieces; 20th-century classics by Paavo Tynell, Adolf Loos, and Pierre Jeanneret; and a few Continental antiques to leaven the brew. “I just pick things that I like, things that make me happy,” Helen says, pooh-poohing the idea of some grand decorative vision. Her designers would demur. “She has an incredible eye,” Sachs insists. “The more crazy Helen would get, the more Brice liked it.”

#4912. Where Does Joe Burrow Live? Unpacking the Bengals Quarterback’s Real Estate Portfolio

He signed a record-breaking contract with the Cincinnati Bengals in 2023, but where does Joe Burrow live when he’s not on the field?

The NFL quarterback was born in Ames, Iowa, in 1996. His family moved to Ohio when he was eight, and he has resided mostly in the Buckeye State ever since. Burrow played for Ohio State University from 2015 to 2017, then transferred as a graduate student to Louisiana State University, where he won the Heisman Trophy shortly before graduating in December 2019. He was drafted into the NFL the following year by his hometown Bengals, with whom he inked a $36.1 million, four-year contract—plus a $23.9 million signing bonus. Three years later Burrow signed a $275 million five-year extension, making him the highest-paid player in NFL history at the time, according to ESPN.

It’s unsurprising, then, that Burrow has put down roots in the Buckeye State. Below, we’re examining the quarterback’s real estate portfolio.

In May 2020, a month after being selected first overall in the NFL Draft, Burrow revealed that he was spending the pandemic lockdown in his old bedroom at his parents’ house in The Plains, Ohio, just outside of Athens. Interior design apparently wasn’t at the forefront of his mind; the room still had his childhood Star Wars curtains and posters on the wall, though he had given the bed a king-size upgrade in high school, replacing the Star Wars comforter that once rounded out the room’s theme. According to The Sun, the 1997-built residence sits on a cul-de-sac and has four bedrooms and three bathrooms.

The Bengals play at Paycor Stadium, formerly known as Paul Brown Stadium.

In June 2020, Burrow spent $835,000 on his first house: a 2,900-square-foot Cincinnati dwelling just five miles from the Bengals’ home stadium. Located in the city’s historic Columbia-Tusculum area, the two-story property was built in 2014. Further details on the dwelling are scant—including whether or not Burrow still owns it. However, its location would make it a convenient place to stay during the NFL season.

#4910. German lawmakers back crypto freezes outside criminal cases

Customs authorities could hold “suspicious” assets for 30 days under the bill, with court oversight for extensions and disputed confiscation.

Germany’s lower house of parliament has passed a bill that would let customs authorities temporarily freeze cryptocurrency and other high-value assets suspected of having unlawful origins without first opening a criminal investigation.

The Bundestag passed the customs reform bill on Friday as part of a wider effort to combat money laundering and organized crime. The proposed procedure would target assets worth more than 100,000 euros and explicitly mentions cryptocurrencies.

Under the bill’s text approved by lawmakers, authorities would be able to hold assets for up to 30 days where there are factual indications of unlawful origins, according to a translated version. However, filing an application for confiscation could suspend those deadlines pending a court decision, and in contested cases, a court would have to be satisfied that the assets were of unlawful origin before ordering confiscation, effectively putting the burden of proof on the crypto holder.

German Social Democratic Party lawmaker Ingo Vogel said that the powers would allow authorities to pursue suspicious assets even when there are not yet grounds to open a criminal case, according to the Bundestag’s summary of the debate on the bill.

The bill still requires consent from the Bundesrat, Germany’s upper house of parliament, and is intended to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Germany’s Federal Bar Association, known as BRAK, previously opposed the government’s draft in an Oct. 28 statement, warning that the meaning of unlawful origin is too vague and risks treating missing records as evidence of illicit wealth.

The association pointed to assets inherited through generations as one example where owners may lack a paper trail. It also questioned what the administrative process would add to Germany’s existing criminal confiscation rules.

German blockchain industry association Bundesblock also raised concerns about the treatment of digital assets in a March 31 submission on an earlier draft. It warned at the time that blockchain analysis should not automatically be treated as proof of ownership or control, and that incorrect wallet attribution could even infringe fundamental rights.

Related: Crypto adoption blooming in Germany, while UK is falling ‘behind,’ says CoinShares researcher

Germany has already carried out large crypto seizures under existing law. As Cointelegraph reported, Saxony authorities sold 49,858 Bitcoin (BTC) linked to the Movie2k piracy investigation in 2024, raising about 2.6 billion euros, or $2.8 billion. At the time, prosecutors said the proceeds remained secured pending a court ruling on confiscation.

In a recent development, local outlet MDR reported on Friday that a Leipzig judge proposed ending proceedings against the main defendant in exchange for 40,000 BTC and a payment of 38 million euros for the potential victims. The proposal remains under consideration.

#4908. The Six Bells Madewell Collection 2026

Whimsical design flourishes, cozy interiors, and close proximity to upstate antiquing all make The Six Bells Countryside Inn one of the best weekend escapes in the Empire State. Now, thanks to Madewell, you never have to check out. Launching today, the two brands have joined forces on a 28-piece holiday capsule of heirloom-worthy wardrobe and home essentials inspired by The Six Bells’ vintage aesthetic. Pieces specifically pay homage to the hotel’s interiors through references to archival patterns and wallpaper prints found throughout the Inn’s rooms and communal spaces.

“We fell in love with [The Six Bells’] distinct, whimsical world—the mix of patterns, the nostalgic sentiment, and the personality in every detail,” says Madewell creative director Steven Cateron. During initial planning for the clothing brand’s holiday collection, the hotel in Rosendale, New York became an unexpected source of inspiration for Cateron and his team because of the shared appreciation for heritage and storytelling. “Each piece has intention, whether it’s to wear day-to-day or for a celebration, a gifting moment for a loved one or hostess, or pajama pieces that lean into cozy season,” he says.

Sock slippers from the collaboration and Madewell’s classic denim make a perfect pairing.

Founded by Audrey Gelman in 2025, who designed the hotel in collaboration with interiors firm GrecoDeco, The Six Bells Countryside Inn has quickly risen in popularity—even earning a spot in AD’s list of Great Design Hotels last year. “This project is so rooted in a shared love of the decorative arts and global human history,” designer Adam Greco previously told AD. Design-wise, maximalism dominates the interiors. Picture: rooms wrapped in fretwork wallpaper and deep cinnabar paint, with pistachio window shades and striped seating.

The collection also builds on the fantasy of Barrow’s Green, the fictional English village dreamed up by Gelman that includes its own imaginary landmarks and distinct locals (including a town gossip and poignant editor). “It was so interesting to broaden our imaginations and think about how The Six Bells’ style could be brought to life through clothes,” says Gelman.

A cheeky message makes this classic needlepoint pillow pop.

At the same time, the collaboration was an opportunity to venture into Madwell’s less-explored categories—specifically the home space. The collection’s interior goods are a practice in curated nostalgia: There are holiday ornaments you’ll reach for year after year, scented candles and soaps to integrate into your daily winter routine, and cozy pajamas inspired by vintage sleep silhouettes. “If it’s something we don’t currently offer, we want to work with people that do the category best,” says Cateron. “The Six Bells team were the perfect partners to bring this collection’s home accessories to life.”

Still, versatility isn’t lost in the assortment. In designing the clothing, Cateron made sure to include “pieces to wear upstate, in the city, or for day-to-day celebrations.” Classic denim jackets are neutral staples that you can reach for any day of the week, while Fair Isle wool knits are seasonally appropriate while still feeling adaptable enough to wear after the holidays. “There’s a real point of view behind every detail [at The Six Bells Countryside Inn], from the interiors to collected vintage pieces,” says Cateron. “This collection captures that sensibility in a way that felt authentic to both brands.”

The collection is available to shop on Madewell.com and in Madewell stores starting today, November 12.

“There’s so much character in every detail at The Six Bells, and we wanted to bring that sensibility into each piece,” says Madewell creative director Steven Cateron.
